docs.title: Connection Issues
docs.text:
Problem: "Invalid Personal Access Token"

Solution: - Ensure token has repo and read:org scopes - Check token hasn't expired - Verify token is for the correct GitHub account

Problem: OAuth callback fails

Solution: - Disconnect and reconnect GitHub from Settings → Integrations - If you use a GitHub organization with third-party app restrictions, ask an org owner to approve the WhiteBoxXAI app - Clear browser cache and try again

docs.title: Webhook Issues
docs.text:
Problem: Webhook shows "Inactive"

Solution: - Click "Setup Webhook" button - Verify repository permissions (admin access required) - Check webhook configuration in GitHub repository settings

Problem: Models not auto-registering

Solution: - Verify .whiteboxxai.yml exists in repository root - Check auto-register is enabled on the tracked repository, and enabled isn't false in .whiteboxxai.yml - Ensure model files match path patterns - Review webhook delivery logs in GitHub repository settings

docs.title: Permission Issues
docs.text:
Problem: "403 Forbidden" when accessing repositories

Solution: - Reconnect GitHub account with correct permissions - For PAT: Regenerate token with repo scope - For OAuth: Re-authorize with repository access

docs.title: Token Encryption
docs.text: All GitHub access tokens (OAuth and PAT) are encrypted at rest using Fernet symmetric encryption (AES-128-CBC).

docs.title: Webhook Signature Verification
docs.text: All webhook payloads are verified using HMAC-SHA256 signatures before processing. Invalid signatures are rejected.

docs.title: Minimal Permissions
docs.text: WhiteBoxXAI requests only necessary permissions: - repo: Repository access (read-only for most operations) - read:org: Organization membership (for organization repositories)

docs.title: Token Revocation
docs.text:
You can revoke WhiteBoxXAI's access anytime:

OAuth: Visit github.com/settings/applications and revoke WhiteBoxXAI

PAT: Delete the connection in WhiteBoxXAI settings, then delete the token in GitHub settings

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use OAuth for interactive use (web dashboard)
  2. Use PAT for automation (CI/CD, scripts)
  3. Rotate PATs regularly (every 90 days recommended)
  4. Use fine-grained PATs when available (GitHub feature)
  5. Monitor connection status and verify periodically
  6. Review webhook logs for unusual activity

docs.title: Hugging Face Transformers
docs.text:
TransformersMonitor logs predictions from Hugging Face Transformers pipelines (text classification, sentiment analysis, token classification, question answering, text generation, summarization and translation) so WhiteBoxXAI can track drift and behaviour over time.

For generative models used as LLMs (chat, RAG, agents), log calls with LLM monitoring instead, which records prompts, completions, tokens and safety scans.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install "whitebox-xai-sdk[huggingface]"

docs.title: Register, then wrap a pipeline
docs.text:
import os

from transformers import pipeline
from whiteboxxai import WhiteBoxXAI
from whiteboxxai.integrations.transformers import TransformersMonitor, wrap_transformers_pipeline

client = WhiteBoxXAI(api_key=os.environ["WHITEBOX_API_KEY"])

classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")

registered = client.models.register(
    name="support-ticket-sentiment",
    model_type="neural_network",
    framework="transformers",
    version="1.0.0",
    features=["text"],
    baseline_metrics={},          # add metrics you measured on your own test set
)

monitor = TransformersMonitor(client, pipeline=classifier, model_id=registered["id"])
classifier = wrap_transformers_pipeline(classifier, monitor)

classifier("The update fixed my issue, thanks!")    # logged

Or let the monitor register it

monitor.register_from_model(name="support-ticket-sentiment", features=["text"]) registers the model and returns its id. model_type defaults to llm for generation tasks (text generation, translation, summarization) and neural_network otherwise, and version defaults to 1.0.0. Pass baseline_metrics={...} once you have measured some on your own test set.

docs.title: Log without wrapping
docs.text:
result = monitor.predict("Where is my refund?")      # runs the pipeline and logs
monitor.log_prediction_transformers(input_text=text, prediction=result)
monitor.log_batch_transformers(inputs=texts, predictions=results)

docs.title: Text generation
docs.text:
For generation pipelines, record what was generated and how long it took:

monitor.log_generation_metrics(
    prompt=prompt,
    generated_text=output,
    num_tokens=num_new_tokens,
    generation_time=elapsed_seconds,
)

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Log the input text the model actually received, and no more. Mask personal data first; see Privacy helpers.
  • Pin the model revision you load, and register a new WhiteBoxXAI version when you change it, so drift and audits refer to the model that produced them.

docs.title: LangChain Multi-Agent
docs.text:
When several agents collaborate (a supervisor routing to specialists, a researcher handing off to a writer, a LangGraph graph of agent nodes), a reviewer needs to see who did what, in what order, and at what cost. WhiteBoxXAI records the run as a multi-agent workflow:

  • the agents taking part, with their roles and models
  • the tasks they worked on and how each ended
  • each agent's executions, and the handoffs between agents
  • every LLM call each agent made, through the LangChain callback handler

After the run, WhiteBoxXAI computes per-agent cost, bottlenecks and a timeline. Runs appear under Observability → Agents in the dashboard. Each workflow is one Governance Event, however many agents and steps it has.

A shorter route: the helpers

This page uses client.agent_workflows so every call is visible. The helpers in whiteboxxai.integrations.langchain_agents wrap the same calls:

from whiteboxxai.integrations.langchain_agents import LangGraphMultiAgentMonitor

monitor = LangGraphMultiAgentMonitor(client, workflow_name="claims-triage")
workflow_id = monitor.start_monitoring(inputs={"claim_id": "CLM-2291"})
monitor.register_agent("triage", role="Classifies the claim", model_name="gpt-4o")
callbacks = monitor.get_callbacks("triage")       # pass as config={"callbacks": callbacks}
monitor.log_handoff("triage", "fraud-check", message="Claim classified")
monitor.complete_monitoring(outputs={"decision": "approve"})

MultiAgentCallbackHandler(client, workflow_id, agent_name="triage") is the per-agent callback handler behind get_callbacks, and monitor_langchain_agent(client, agent_executor, workflow_name) runs a single agent as a one-agent workflow and returns its result and workflow_id.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install "whitebox-xai-sdk[langchain]" langgraph langchain-openai

docs.title: Record a run
docs.text:
import os

from whiteboxxai import WhiteBoxXAI
from whiteboxxai.integrations.langchain import LangChainMonitor, WhiteBoxXAICallbackHandler

client = WhiteBoxXAI(api_key=os.environ["WHITEBOX_API_KEY"])
wf = client.agent_workflows

# 1. Create the workflow (this is the one Governance Event)
workflow = wf.create_and_start(name="claims-triage", framework="langchain",
                               meta_data={"ticket": "CLM-2291"})
workflow_id = workflow["id"]

# 2. Register the agents
triage = wf.register_agent(workflow_id, name="triage", role="Classifies the claim",
                           model_name="gpt-4o", llm_provider="openai")
fraud = wf.register_agent(workflow_id, name="fraud-check", role="Checks for fraud signals",
                          model_name="claude-sonnet-4-6", llm_provider="anthropic")

# 3. Start the run
wf.start(workflow_id, inputs={"claim_id": "CLM-2291"})

# 4. LLM calls from every agent are logged by the LangChain callback handler
handler = WhiteBoxXAICallbackHandler(LangChainMonitor(client, application_name="claims-triage"))

Then, while the graph or agents run, record what happens:

# A task assigned to an agent
task = wf.create_task(workflow_id, task_name="Classify claim", agent_id=triage["id"],
                      input_data={"claim_id": "CLM-2291"})

# The agent starts work
execution = wf.create_execution(workflow_id, agent_id=triage["id"],
                                inputs={"claim_id": "CLM-2291"}, execution_order=1)

result = triage_agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", claim_text)]},
                             config={"callbacks": [handler]})

# The task's outcome
wf.update_task_status(task["id"], status="completed", output_data={"category": "water damage"})

# A handoff from one agent to another
wf.log_interaction(workflow_id, interaction_type="delegation",
                   from_agent_id=triage["id"], to_agent_id=fraud["id"],
                   from_execution_id=execution["id"],
                   message="Claim classified; check for duplicate submissions")

Finally, complete the workflow, including when it fails, so it isn't left running:

wf.complete(workflow_id, status="completed", outputs={"decision": "approve"})
# or: wf.complete(workflow_id, status="failed", error_message=str(err))

Steps after create_and_start (agents, tasks, executions, interactions and completion) are free.

docs.title: With LangGraph
docs.text:
Record agents once, when you build the graph, and add the handoff in the node that routes between agents:

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END

def route(state):
    nxt = "fraud" if state["needs_fraud_check"] else END
    if nxt != END:
        wf.log_interaction(workflow_id, interaction_type="handoff",
                           from_agent_id=triage["id"], to_agent_id=fraud["id"],
                           message="Routing to fraud check")
    return nxt

graph = StateGraph(ClaimState)
graph.add_node("triage", triage_node)
graph.add_node("fraud", fraud_node)
graph.set_entry_point("triage")
graph.add_conditional_edges("triage", route)
app = graph.compile()

app.invoke({"claim": claim_text}, config={"callbacks": [handler]})

Interaction types used in practice include delegation, handoff, message and tool_call.

docs.title: Read the analytics
docs.text:
Analytics are computed after complete and may take a short while to be ready:

wf.analytics(workflow_id)          # tokens, costs, execution counts, durations
wf.cost_breakdown(workflow_id)     # per agent
wf.bottlenecks(workflow_id)        # slowest agents and tasks, failing agents
wf.timeline(workflow_id)           # every event in order

cost_breakdown, bottlenecks and timeline can take up to about 30 seconds.

docs.title: LangChain
docs.text:
The WhiteBoxXAI callback handler records what a LangChain or LangGraph application does: each LLM call (model, prompt, completion, tokens, latency), chain runs, tool calls and errors. It works with any LangChain chat model, so OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, Bedrock, Ollama and the rest are all covered.

Each root run's records are sent as one governance run, so a run with a dozen LLM calls costs one Governance Event, not twelve.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install "whitebox-xai-sdk[langchain]" langchain-openai     # or langchain-anthropic, langchain-google-genai, ...

docs.title: Set up the handler
docs.text:
Register the application as an LLM system once, then create a monitor for it and a callback handler:

import os

from whiteboxxai import WhiteBoxXAI
from whiteboxxai.integrations.langchain import LangChainMonitor, WhiteBoxXAICallbackHandler

client = WhiteBoxXAI(api_key=os.environ["WHITEBOX_API_KEY"])

app = client.models.register(
    name="support-assistant",
    model_type="llm",
    framework="langchain",
    version="1.4.0",
    features=["question"],
    baseline_metrics={},
)

monitor = LangChainMonitor(client, application_name="support-assistant", model_id=app["id"])
handler = WhiteBoxXAICallbackHandler(monitor)

Or let the monitor register it

monitor.register_application(name="support-assistant", version="1.4.0", features=["question"]) registers the application as an llm system and returns its id, and monitor.create_callback_handler() then returns the same handler as WhiteBoxXAICallbackHandler(monitor). If the application isn't registered yet, create_callback_handler() registers it with defaults (version 1.0.0, one input named input), so register it yourself when you want real versions and input names. The name may contain only letters, digits, spaces, - and _; the API rejects other characters.

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
Pass the handler in the run config. It works with chains, chat models, agents and LangGraph graphs:

from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You answer customer questions using the policy excerpts provided."),
    ("human", "{question}"),
])
chain = prompt | ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o")

answer = chain.invoke(
    {"question": "Can I get a refund after 30 days?"},
    config={"callbacks": [handler]},
)

Swap ChatOpenAI for ChatAnthropic, ChatGoogleGenerativeAI, ChatMistralAI, ChatBedrock, ChatOllama or any other LangChain chat model; logging is the same.

For a LangGraph graph or agent:

result = graph.invoke({"messages": [("user", question)]}, config={"callbacks": [handler]})

For multi-agent systems where you want agents, tasks and agent-to-agent interactions recorded as a workflow, see LangChain Multi-Agent.

docs.title: What's recorded
docs.text:
Event Recorded as LLM call An LLM log: provider, model, prompt, completion, tokens, latency, status Chain or graph run A chain execution on the registered application, with inputs, outputs and duration Tool call The tool name, input, output and duration Errors The failure, on the call or run it belongs to

LLM calls appear in the LLM & RAG audit trail.

docs.title: Log retrievals
docs.text:
If your RAG chain retrieves documents, log the retrieval so retrieval quality is tracked:

monitor.log_rag_retrieval(
    query=question,
    documents=[{"document_id": d.metadata["id"], "content": d.page_content} for d in docs],
    num_retrieved=len(docs),
    relevance_scores=scores,
    ground_truth_ids=["kb-17"],    # optional: enables precision, recall, MRR and NDCG
    answer=answer.content,
)

docs.title: Add safety scans and prompt versions
docs.text:
client.safety.analyze(content=answer.content, content_type="completion")

Governed prompt versions are managed with client.prompts; link the calls they produce by logging with prompt_version_id. See Evaluations & Prompt Versions.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Nothing appears. Check the handler is in config={"callbacks": [...]} on the invoke call (or attached to the model), and that WHITEBOX_API_KEY is set in the process running the chain.

Costs are blank. Cost is calculated only for model names WhiteBoxXAI has prices for. See LLM monitoring.

docs.title: LiteLLM gateway
docs.text:
If your teams call models through a LiteLLM proxy, that proxy already sees every request, but nothing records those requests as governance evidence. Each team would have to add WhiteBoxXAI logging to its own code, and the ones that don't are the ones you can't see.

Connecting the gateway moves the recording to the one place every call passes through. An organisation administrator connects it once in Settings → LLM gateway, adds one block to LiteLLM's configuration, and from then on each call is stored in WhiteBoxXAI and filed under the AI system it belongs to. Nobody changes their own code.

This page is written against LiteLLM 1.106.6. It records what the gateway sends; it does not check that the gateway sends everything. See What it cannot see.

docs.title: How the data gets here
docs.text:
LiteLLM has a built-in callback, generic_api, that posts batches of its standard logging records to any HTTPS endpoint. WhiteBoxXAI is that endpoint. LiteLLM pushes; WhiteBoxXAI does not poll your gateway, and never holds your LiteLLM master key.

LiteLLM proxy ── POST /api/v1/llm/gateways/litellm/ingest ──► WhiteBoxXAI
   (batch of up to 512 calls,                                  maps each call, applies your
    sent every 5 seconds)                                      content policy, files it

The gateway authenticates with its own token, which starts wbx_lgw_. It is not an API key: an API key acts with the permissions of the administrator who made it, and a key pasted into a gateway configuration file would carry all of them. The gateway token can do one thing, which is send calls for your organisation.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
You need to be an administrator of your organisation. The gateway works on every plan; its calls count as Governance Events.

  1. Connect. In Settings → LLM gateway, on the LiteLLM tab, name the gateway and choose what is stored from each call (see What is stored), then select Connect LiteLLM. WhiteBoxXAI shows a token once. Copy it now; if you lose it, rotate it.

  2. Paste the configuration into LiteLLM's config.yaml. The pane shows this block with your deployment's address filled in:

    litellm_settings:
  callbacks: ["whiteboxxai"]
  # Requests sent with the no-log flag would otherwise never reach WhiteBox.
  global_disable_no_log_param: true

callback_settings:
  whiteboxxai:
    callback_type: generic_api
    endpoint: os.environ/WHITEBOXXAI_INGEST_URL
    headers:
      Authorization: os.environ/WHITEBOXXAI_AUTHORIZATION
    event_types: ["llm_api_success", "llm_api_failure"]
    log_format: json_array
    max_retries: 3
    retry_delay: 2
    timeout: 30

  3. Set two environment variables where LiteLLM runs:

    Variable Value WHITEBOXXAI_INGEST_URL https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/llm/gateways/litellm/ingest (shown in the pane; a Business Cloud tenant has its own address) WHITEBOXXAI_AUTHORIZATION Bearer wbx_lgw_..., the whole header value including the word Bearer

  4. Restart LiteLLM, send a request through it, and wait about ten seconds. The pane changes from "Waiting for the first call" to "Receiving".

An organisation has one LiteLLM connection. If you run several LiteLLM proxies, give them all the same configuration and token; their calls arrive as one gateway.

The pane also has tabs for OpenTelemetry (OTLP), Portkey AI, Kong AI Gateway and Azure APIM. Those are covered in LLM gateways.

docs.title: Three details that matter
docs.text:
• Use callbacks, not success_callback. With success_callback or failure_callback, LiteLLM builds the logger and prints that it initialised it, but never calls it: nothing is sent and neither side reports an error. event_types still limits the callback to the two events listed.
  • Keep the retry settings. LiteLLM's default is no retries, and a batch that fails once is thrown away. With max_retries set, LiteLLM retries timeouts, connection errors and server errors. It does not retry a refusal (see When calls are lost).
  • global_disable_no_log_param: true makes LiteLLM ignore the per-request switches that turn logging off, including the x-litellm-disable-callbacks header. Without it, a request sent with no-log never reaches WhiteBoxXAI.

docs.title: What is stored
docs.text:
You choose, per gateway, and can change it later. A change applies to calls received from then on; calls already recorded keep the policy they were recorded under, and each row says which one that was.

Policy Stored Redact personal data (recommended), the default Prompts, responses, messages and tool calls, with the patterns below removed. Metadata only No prompt, response, message, tool definition or tool call. You keep who called which model, tokens, cost, timing and the class of any error. Store everything as sent Exactly what the gateway sent, personal data included.

docs.title: What redaction removes, and what it does not
docs.text:
Redaction matches patterns. It does not understand the text, so it has limits, and the pane states them next to the choice.

It removes: email addresses, US-format phone numbers, 16-digit card numbers, US Social Security numbers, IPv4 addresses, API keys, access tokens and private keys, and embedded images and files.

It does not find: names, postal addresses, phone numbers outside the US, American Express and other card numbers that are not 16 digits, IBANs, and national ID numbers. If those must never be held, choose Metadata only.

It walks every string in the call, including chat messages made of typed blocks and the arguments of tool calls. Each stored row records which policy applied, the method (pattern_v1), and the kinds of thing it removed.

docs.title: What is recorded from each call
docs.text:
LiteLLM sends Stored as custom_llm_provider Provider model Model name, as LiteLLM names it (for example openai/gpt-4o) messages, response Messages, prompt (the last user turn) and completion, under your policy prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens Token counts response_cost Cost, as LiteLLM reports it. WhiteBoxXAI does not re-estimate it. If LiteLLM sends none, the cost is recorded as unavailable, not as zero. startTime, endTime Time of the call and latency status, error_information Outcome: success, failure, timeout or rate-limited, with the error litellm_call_id Request id, used to recognise a retried batch request_tags, session_id, end_user Tags (including any LiteLLM adds itself, such as User-Agent), session, and the end user model_parameters Temperature, maximum tokens, top-p, penalties, and tool definitions key alias, team, team id, model group The labels used to file the call under an AI system

Never stored: the hash of the LiteLLM key, the key owner's email, the requester's IP address, custom request headers, request metadata the caller attached, LiteLLM's spend-log metadata (spend_logs_metadata), and LiteLLM's internal parameters. The address of the model endpoint is kept without any credentials or query string.

docs.title: Filing calls under AI systems
docs.text:
A call is stored the moment it arrives. Which AI system it belongs to is decided by rules, evaluated lowest priority number first, then oldest first:

  • A rule maps a label to an AI system. The labels are the team, team ID, API key and model that LiteLLM reports, and tags.
  • A default AI system, if you set one, takes every call that matches no rule. Use it only if one system really owns everything else, because it hides the traffic nobody has claimed.
  • A call that matches nothing is still stored, with no AI system.

Team and key labels exist only if you use LiteLLM's virtual keys and teams. Without them, the only label a call has is its model, and that is all the pane can list.

docs.title: Unregistered traffic
docs.text:
The pane lists, for the last 30 days, each team, key, model and tag label that no rule claims, with its call count and when it was last seen. For a risk officer this is the answer to "what is flowing through our gateway that nobody registered". A call can appear under several labels at once, so the per-label counts add up to more than the number of calls; the heading shows the real figure as "(N distinct calls)".

If your calls carry no team or API key, the pane says so: only the model is known, and an assignment applies to everything sent to that model. If you have set a default AI system, the pane shows how many calls it has absorbed in the last 30 days, so the traffic it hides is still counted.

To claim a label, choose an AI system next to it and select Assign. If the system isn't registered yet, register it and come back. To write a rule for a label that isn't listed, use Add rule: pick the field (Tag, Team, Team ID, API key or Model), enter the value, choose the AI system.

Assigning also files the last 30 days of unassigned matching calls under that system. It runs in the background. The pane checks back for a few seconds and then says how many earlier calls were assigned, or that they are still being assigned. Each re-filed call is stamped with how and when it was attributed (retroactive, the rule, who assigned it), so the record shows a link made after the fact. A call that already has an AI system is not moved. Removing a rule affects calls received from then on; calls already filed keep their AI system.

docs.title: Health
docs.text:
The pane leads with a verdict in words, then what to do, then the counts.

State Meaning What to do Waiting for the first call Nothing has arrived. Check the configuration, the two variables, and that LiteLLM was restarted. Receiving Calls are arriving. Nothing. Receiving, with problems Calls arrive, but some records were rejected as unreadable. The reason is shown. Usually a LiteLLM setting that changes the record format; see Troubleshooting. Calls are being lost Batches were refused before they were recorded. The count of calls not recorded is shown. See When calls are lost. Gone quiet It was receiving, and nothing has arrived for 24 hours. Check the gateway is running and its configuration is unchanged. Disabled You switched acceptance off. Switch it back on.

The counts are totals since you connected: calls recorded, records rejected, and calls lost before they arrived. The LLM gateways card on Settings → Integrations shows the verdict too, so a gateway that has stopped is visible without opening the pane. If you have connected more than one gateway, the card shows whichever needs attention most, and names it.

docs.title: When calls are lost
docs.text:
Two things refuse a batch before it is recorded: a Free plan that has used its monthly Governance Events, and the gateway's rate limit of 1,200 requests per 60 seconds. Both answer 429. LiteLLM does not resend a refused batch, so those calls are not in your evidence record. WhiteBoxXAI cannot recover them, but it does count them and says why, which is the part that would otherwise be silent.

A request that is too large (413, see Limits) is also counted as lost, but it does not change the verdict to Calls are being lost; only quota and rate-limit refusals do.

On Business Cloud the monthly allowance is not a hard cap, so only the rate limit applies.

docs.title: What it cannot see
docs.text:
WhiteBoxXAI records what the gateway sends. It cannot check that against anything.

  • A call that does not go through a connected gateway is invisible: a team calling a provider directly, or a second gateway that isn't connected.
  • A gateway whose configuration changed after setup, or that is stopped, sends nothing. A stopped gateway shows as Gone quiet after 24 hours, not before.
  • There is no reconciliation against LiteLLM's own spend logs. It would catch a gap in either direction, and is not built yet.

So the pane says "Every call received in the last 30 days belongs to an AI system you have registered" only when calls have arrived and none is unassigned. It never says every call is recorded.

docs.title: Governance Events
docs.text: Each call that is stored is one Governance Event, the same as a call logged by the SDK. A call that is a duplicate (LiteLLM re-sending a batch) or that WhiteBoxXAI rejected as unreadable costs nothing. See Governance Events.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Records per request 1,000. LiteLLM sends up to 512 by default, so you only reach this if you raise DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE. A larger request is refused with 413 and counted as lost. Request size 32 MB. A larger body is refused with 413 and counted as lost. Request rate 1,200 per 60 seconds per gateway, separate from your dashboard and SDK traffic Retention Recorded calls follow your organisation's data retention policy, the same as calls logged with the SDK: 90 days on Free, 365 days by default on paid plans, which can be set between 1 and 7 years. Calls older than 30 days are compressed in storage. An administrator can remove older calls sooner with DELETE /api/v1/llm/logs/cleanup?days=N (days from 1 to 365), which only touches their own organisation.

docs.title: Manage the connection
docs.text:
• Rotate the token replaces it. The old one stops working immediately, so the gateway is refused, and its calls lost, until you put the new token in WHITEBOXXAI_AUTHORIZATION. Rotating needs an administrator on a signed-in session, not an API key.
  • Accept calls from this gateway switched off makes WhiteBoxXAI refuse everything it sends.
  • Disconnect removes the LiteLLM connection and its rules. Calls already recorded are kept, and a gateway connected on another tab is not affected.

Every change, including connecting, rotating, each rule and each re-filing of earlier calls, is recorded in the audit trail. The token is never written to it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: You see Cause Still "Waiting for the first call" The configuration uses success_callback instead of callbacks; LiteLLM wasn't restarted; or the variables aren't set where LiteLLM runs. LiteLLM's debug log (--detailed_debug) shows Generic API Logger - sent batch ... status: 200 when it works. 401 in LiteLLM's log The token is wrong, was rotated, or the connection is disabled. WhiteBoxXAI answers all three the same way. "Receiving, with problems" and startTime/endTime are not numbers LiteLLM's generic_api_use_v1 is on, which sends an older record shape. Turn it off. 413 A request carried more than 1,000 records. Lower DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE. 429 A quota or rate-limit refusal; see When calls are lost. Calls arrive with no AI system No rule matches. Assign the label under Unregistered traffic.

docs.title: Without the pane
docs.text:
The endpoint accepts LiteLLM's default json_array body: a JSON array of standard logging records, with Authorization: Bearer wbx_lgw_.... It returns how many were stored:

{ "accepted": 12, "duplicates": 0, "rejected": 0 }

A record it cannot read is counted in rejected and the rest of the batch is still stored, because an error status would make LiteLLM resend the whole batch. A single record object is accepted too, for LiteLLM's single log format. The administrator endpoints are under /api/v1/integrations/llm-gateways/litellm; see the API reference.

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text:
The WhiteBoxXAI MCP server is the MCP Governance Layer for AI assistants and agents. It gives any Model Context Protocol client (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, LangChain or Semantic Kernel agents, or your own harness) 197 tools over your WhiteBoxXAI data. With them, an assistant can register models, log predictions and LLM calls, check drift, explain predictions, run bias audits, triage alerts, read ISO/IEC 42001 readiness and the risk register, summarise governance review requests, and manage prompt versions.

Every tool calls the real WhiteBoxXAI API. None returns mocked or placeholder data. When something can't be computed, the tool says so.

Writing Python application code? Use the SDK instead. The MCP server is for assistants and agents that use WhiteBoxXAI as a tool.

Let your coding agent set this up

The whitebox-mcp-server skill teaches an agent to install and configure the server and pick the right tool. Load it with whitebox-governance-rules.

docs.title: Two ways to connect
docs.text: Local (stdio) Hosted (Streamable HTTP) What runs where whiteboxxai-mcp runs on your machine; your client starts it Nothing to install; your client connects to https://api.whiteboxxai.com/mcp/ Credential An API key in WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_API_KEY An Authorization: Bearer header on every request: an API key or a personal sign-in token Governance voting Not available Available with a personal sign-in token Best for Coding assistants and agents in your own environment Clients that support remote MCP servers, and interactive voting

docs.title: Install (local)
docs.text:
Requires Python 3.11 or later.

pip install whiteboxxai-mcp

Create an API key in Settings → API keys (administrators only; see API Keys), then check the server starts:

export WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_API_KEY="wbx_live_..."
whiteboxxai-mcp

Your MCP client normally starts the command itself; you don't keep it running in a terminal.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_API_KEY none (required) Your API key (wbx_live_...) WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_API_BASE_URL https://api.whiteboxxai.com Your API address. Business Cloud tenants use the address they were given. WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_API_TIMEOUT 30 Request timeout, in seconds WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_LOG_LEVEL Log level, for example DEBUG

whiteboxxai-mcp --verbose (or WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_VERBOSE=1) logs request and response metadata, never credential values.

The local server authenticates only with an API key. If none is set, it exits with code 2 and whiteboxxai-mcp: no credentials configured.

docs.title: Connect a client
Hosted endpoint authentication
docs.text:
• Every request needs its own Authorization: Bearer <token> header: an API key, or a personal sign-in token. There's no fallback to environment variables, and a request without a valid header is refused with 401 before a session starts.
  • Clients or gateways that can't set Authorization (some registries and proxies reserve it) can send an API key in an X-WhiteBox-API-Key: wbx_live_... header instead. If a request carries both, X-WhiteBox-API-Key is used. The header was added in whiteboxxai-mcp 0.3.2.
  • A personal sign-in token expires after about 30 minutes and isn't refreshed by the server. Reconnect with a fresh token, or use an API key for long-running sessions.
  • Activity sent with an API key is metered as Governance Events in the same way as SDK calls.

docs.title: MCP Apps: interactive cards
docs.text:
In clients that support MCP Apps, some results render as interactive cards inside the conversation instead of raw JSON:

Card Shown for Explanation card whitebox_explanations_generate, _get, _get_by_prediction Alert triage card whitebox_alerts_get_instance, whitebox_alerts_get_triage_context, whitebox_drift_get_report Governance dossier card whitebox_governance_list_review_requests, _get_review_request, _submit_decision ISO/IEC 42001 status card whitebox_compliance_iso42001_score, _gaps, _status Model version diff card whitebox_models_compare_versions, _version_changelog, _architecture_timeline

How the cards are built:

  • Each card is a sandboxed ui://whitebox/... resource with a strict content security policy: it can't load anything from the network and holds no credentials. Buttons on a card ask your client to call a tool; they don't call WhiteBoxXAI directly.
  • The card and the text result carry the same data and the same plain-language verdict. Clients without MCP Apps support get the full JSON result.
  • Explanation cards replace common personal data patterns, such as email addresses and phone numbers, with [REDACTED:<TYPE>] before display.

docs.title: Governance voting
docs.text:
The governance tools let an assistant prepare a review: list what's waiting, open a request's dossier (board, submitter, decisions, comments, vote tally and its evidence snapshot hash), and summarise it. Casting the vote stays with a person:

  • whitebox_governance_submit_decision is an app-only tool. It's hidden from the model and only offered as a button on the governance dossier card, so an assistant can't vote on its own.
  • A vote needs your own sign-in token on the hosted endpoint. An organization API key is refused, and so is the local stdio server, which only uses API keys.
  • Every vote needs a current authenticator code, and two-factor authentication must be on.
  • The vote carries the evidence snapshot hash of the dossier you saw. If the request changed since, it's refused with 409, and you review the current version first.

See Reviews & Decisions.

docs.title: Example prompts
docs.text: Ask the assistant It calls "What models do we have?" whitebox_models_list "Has credit_scoring drifted this month? Keep a record." whitebox_drift_detect, then whitebox_drift_create_report "Why was this prediction declined?" whitebox_explanations_get_by_prediction or whitebox_explanations_generate "What's firing right now, and why?" whitebox_alerts_list_instances, whitebox_alerts_get_triage_context "Where are we on ISO 42001?" whitebox_compliance_iso42001_status "What's waiting for my review?" whitebox_governance_list_review_requests "How did v3 differ from v2?" whitebox_models_compare_versions "Roll back the support-bot prompt to the last verified version." whitebox_prompts_rollback

docs.title: Tool reference
docs.text: Tools are named whitebox_<domain>_<action>, across 18 domains. Required arguments are listed; see each tool's input schema in your client for optional ones.

docs.title: LLM explainability

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text:
• No report generation tools. Generate reports with the SDK or the dashboard. Over MCP, an assistant can create and read drift reports and read the evidence reports draw on.
  • Not every administrative endpoint is a tool. Escalation-policy management and bulk alert actions are left out on purpose. If a tool doesn't exist, the assistant should say so rather than simulate it.
  • Workflow analytics can be slow. whitebox_agent_workflows_cost_breakdown, _bottlenecks and _timeline can take up to about 30 seconds.
  • Hosted sessions with a personal sign-in token expire after about 30 minutes; reconnect with a fresh token, or use an API key where you don't need to vote.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
whiteboxxai-mcp: no credentials configured (exit code 2). Set WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_API_KEY in the environment the client starts the server with, not only in your shell.

401 Unauthorized. The key is mistyped, revoked or expired, or (on the hosted endpoint) the Authorization header is missing or the sign-in token has expired.

403 on a vote. Votes need your own sign-in token, two-factor authentication and an authenticator code. An API key can't vote.

404 on an id. The record isn't in your organization. Check the id rather than retrying with other credentials.

429. Either the rate limit (wait for Retry-After) or, on the Free plan, the month's Governance Events are used up.

Calls hang, then time out. WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_API_BASE_URL isn't reachable from where the server runs. Check the address and WHITEBOXXAI_MCP_API_TIMEOUT.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Use one API key per client or agent, so you can revoke one without breaking the others.
  • Credential values are never logged; verbose mode logs request metadata only.
  • The server doesn't write model weights or training data anywhere. It only calls the WhiteBoxXAI API.
  • An API key acts with the permissions of the administrator who created it. See API Keys.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The WhiteBoxXAI n8n integration enables monitoring of n8n workflow automation through webhooks. This provides observability into your n8n workflows, tracking node executions, AI agent interactions, and workflow performance.

docs.title: Supported Features
docs.text:
• Workflow Monitoring: Track complete n8n workflow executions from start to finish
  • Node-Level Tracking: Monitor individual node executions with timing and status
  • AI Node Detection: Automatically identify and track AI-powered nodes (OpenAI, AI Agent, etc.)
  • Error Tracking: Capture and log node failures with detailed error information
  • Multi-Tenancy: Organization-scoped workflow tracking with proper isolation
  • Idempotency: Handle duplicate webhook calls gracefully

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
┌─────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐
│  n8n Cloud  │ Webhook │  WhiteBoxXAI API  │  Maps   │   WhiteBoxXAI    │
│     or      ├────────►│   /webhooks/n8n  ├────────►│   Database      │
│ Self-Hosted │  POST   │   /execution     │  Nodes  │  (Workflows)    │
└─────────────┘         └──────────────────┘  to     └─────────────────┘
                                               Agents

Mapping Logic: - n8n Workflow → WhiteBoxXAI Workflow - n8n Node → WhiteBoxXAI Agent - Node Execution → Agent Execution - Workflow Run → Workflow Lifecycle (create → start → complete)

docs.title: 1. Get Webhook Configuration
docs.text:
curl -X GET "https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/webhooks/n8n/config" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"

Response: 

{
  "webhook_url": "https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/webhooks/n8n/execution",
  "track_all_nodes": true,
  "min_execution_time_ms": 0
}

docs.title: 2. Configure n8n Webhook Node
docs.text:
Add a Webhook node to your n8n workflow (at the end to capture completion):

Webhook Configuration: 

{
  "httpMethod": "POST",
  "path": "",
  "responseMode": "onReceived",
  "options": {},
  "authentication": "headerAuth",
  "headerAuth": {
    "name": "Authorization",
    "value": "Bearer wbx_live_..."
  }
}

Set Webhook URL: 

https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/webhooks/n8n/execution

docs.title: 3. Configure Workflow Settings
docs.text:
In your n8n workflow settings, add a Webhook node and configure the payload:

Expression to Send (in HTTP Request body): 

{
  "workflow_id": "{{ $workflow.id }}",
  "workflow_name": "{{ $workflow.name }}",
  "execution_id": "{{ $execution.id }}",
  "status": "{{ $execution.mode === 'manual' && $execution.finished ? 'success' : 'error' }}",
  "started_at": "{{ $execution.startedAt }}",
  "finished_at": "{{ $now }}",
  "mode": "{{ $execution.mode }}",
  "nodes": {{ $json.nodes }},
  "meta_data": {
    "project": "your-project-name",
    "environment": "production"
  }
}

docs.title: 4. Collect Node Data
docs.text:
To send node execution data, add a Code node before the webhook:

// Collect all node execution data
const nodes = [];

for (const itemIndex in items) {
  const item = items[itemIndex];

  // Get all previous nodes
  for (const nodeName of Object.keys($input.all())) {
    const nodeData = $input.all()[nodeName];

    if (nodeData && nodeData.length > 0) {
      nodes.push({
        node_name: nodeName,
        node_type: nodeData[0].json.nodeType || "unknown",
        input_data: nodeData[0].json.input || {},
        output_data: nodeData[0].json,
        execution_time_ms: nodeData[0].json.executionTime || 0,
        status: "success"
      });
    }
  }
}

return [{ json: { nodes } }];

docs.title: Example 1: AI Content Generation Workflow
docs.text:
This n8n workflow uses OpenAI to generate blog content, then checks grammar:

Workflow Structure: 1. Trigger (Manual or Schedule) 2. OpenAI Agent - Generate blog post 3. Grammar Check - Validate content 4. Collect Data (Code node) 5. Send to WhiteBoxXAI (Webhook node)

Code Node (Step 4): 

const workflowId = $workflow.id;
const workflowName = $workflow.name;
const executionId = $execution.id;
const startedAt = new Date($execution.startedAt).toISOString();
const finishedAt = new Date().toISOString();

// Collect node executions
const nodes = [
  {
    node_name: "OpenAI Agent",
    node_type: "n8n-nodes-base.openAi",
    input_data: {
      prompt: "Write a blog post about AI in healthcare"
    },
    output_data: $node["OpenAI Agent"].json,
    execution_time_ms: 2500,
    status: "success"
  },
  {
    node_name: "Grammar Check",
    node_type: "n8n-nodes-base.httpRequest",
    input_data: {
      text: $node["OpenAI Agent"].json.text
    },
    output_data: $node["Grammar Check"].json,
    execution_time_ms: 1200,
    status: "success"
  }
];

return [{
  json: {
    workflow_id: workflowId,
    workflow_name: workflowName,
    execution_id: executionId,
    status: "success",
    started_at: startedAt,
    finished_at: finishedAt,
    mode: $execution.mode,
    nodes: nodes,
    meta_data: {
      project: "content-automation",
      version: "1.0"
    }
  }
}];

Webhook Node (Step 5): - URL: https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/webhooks/n8n/execution - Method: POST - Authentication: Bearer Token (WhiteBoxXAI API Key) - Body: {{ $json }}

docs.title: Example 2: Error Handling
docs.text:
Handle failed nodes in your workflow:

// In Code node - detect failures
const hasError = $execution.mode === 'manual' &&
                 !$execution.finished;

const status = hasError ? "error" : "success";

const nodes = [];
for (const nodeName of Object.keys($input.all())) {
  const nodeData = $input.all()[nodeName];

  // Check if node failed
  const nodeStatus = nodeData[0].json.error ? "error" : "success";
  const error = nodeData[0].json.error || null;

  nodes.push({
    node_name: nodeName,
    node_type: nodeData[0].json.nodeType || "unknown",
    input_data: nodeData[0].json.input || {},
    output_data: nodeData[0].json.error ? {} : nodeData[0].json,
    execution_time_ms: nodeData[0].json.executionTime || 0,
    status: nodeStatus,
    error: error
  });
}

return [{
  json: {
    workflow_id: $workflow.id,
    workflow_name: $workflow.name,
    execution_id: $execution.id,
    status: status,
    started_at: new Date($execution.startedAt).toISOString(),
    finished_at: new Date().toISOString(),
    mode: $execution.mode,
    nodes: nodes
  }
}];

docs.title: Node Type Detection
docs.text:
WhiteBoxXAI automatically detects AI nodes based on node type:

AI Nodes (tracked as AI agents): - n8n-nodes-base.openAi - n8n-nodes-base.openAiChat - *ai* (any node type containing "ai") - Custom AI nodes

Other Nodes (tracked as utility agents): - HTTP Request nodes - Code nodes - Webhook nodes - Database nodes - All other n8n nodes

docs.title: 2. Duplicate Execution Handling
docs.text:
WhiteBoxXAI automatically handles duplicate webhook calls:

  • Checks for existing workflows with same n8n_execution_id in metadata
  • Updates existing workflow instead of creating duplicate
  • Idempotent operations ensure data consistency

docs.title: 3. Workflow Tracking
docs.text:
Each n8n execution is tracked with:

External ID: n8n:{workflow_id}:{execution_id}
Framework: n8n
Status: running → completed/failed

docs.title: 4. Agent Registration
docs.text:
Nodes are automatically registered as agents:

Name: {node_name}
Role: {node_type} (e.g., "OpenAI Agent")
Is AI: true (for AI nodes)

docs.title: 5. Execution Logging
docs.text:
Each node execution is logged with:

  • Input/output data
  • Execution time (ms)
  • Status (success/error/waiting)
  • Error messages (if failed)

docs.title: 1. Webhook Placement
docs.text:
Recommended: Place webhook node at the end of your workflow to capture complete execution data.

[Trigger] → [Node 1] → [Node 2] → [Collect Data] → [WhiteBoxXAI Webhook]

docs.title: 2. Error Handling
docs.text:
Always wrap webhook calls in try-catch to prevent workflow failures:

try {
  // Collect and send data
  const webhookData = { /* ... */ };
  // Send to WhiteBoxXAI
} catch (error) {
  console.error("Failed to send to WhiteBoxXAI:", error);
  // Continue workflow execution
}

docs.title: 3. Data Collection
docs.text: Use a dedicated Code node to collect all node execution data before sending to webhook.

docs.title: 4. Authentication
docs.text:
• Use Bearer Token authentication
  • Store API key in n8n credentials (encrypted)
  • Never hardcode API keys in workflow JSON

docs.title: 5. Rate Limiting
docs.text:
• Webhook calls share the standard API rate limit (100 requests per 60 seconds by default); see Rate limits
  • Send one call per workflow execution rather than one per node
  • Use async webhook mode (responseMode: "onReceived")

docs.title: 6. Metadata
docs.text:
Include relevant metadata for filtering and analysis:

{
  "meta_data": {
    "project": "project-name",
    "environment": "production|staging|dev",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "tags": ["ai", "automation", "content"]
  }
}

docs.title: Issue 1: Webhook Not Receiving Data
docs.text:
Symptoms: No workflows appearing in WhiteBoxXAI dashboard

Solutions: 1. Verify webhook URL is correct 2. Check API key is valid and has correct permissions 3. Verify n8n workflow is actually executing 4. Check n8n webhook node logs for errors 5. Test webhook endpoint manually (see Testing section)

docs.title: Issue 2: Incomplete Node Data
docs.text:
Symptoms: Some nodes not tracked in WhiteBoxXAI

Solutions: 1. Ensure Code node collects all previous nodes 2. Check node execution order 3. Verify all nodes complete before webhook fires 4. Use $input.all() to get all node data

docs.title: Issue 3: Duplicate Workflows
docs.text:
Symptoms: Same execution creating multiple workflows

Solutions: 1. Ensure execution_id is unique and consistent 2. Check for multiple webhook calls in n8n 3. WhiteBoxXAI handles duplicates automatically, but verify n8n configuration

docs.title: Issue 4: Authentication Errors
docs.text:
Symptoms: 401 Unauthorized responses

Solutions: 1. Verify API key format: Bearer wbx_live_... 2. Check organization access for API key 3. Ensure API key has webhooks:write permission 4. Test API key with /api/v1/webhooks/n8n/config endpoint

docs.title: Issue 5: Node Status Not Updating
docs.text:
Symptoms: Workflows stuck in "running" status

Solutions: 1. Ensure status field is set correctly (success or error) 2. Verify finished_at timestamp is sent 3. Check that webhook fires after all nodes complete 4. Review n8n execution mode (manual, trigger, etc.)

docs.title: POST /api/v1/webhooks/n8n/execution
docs.text:
Receive n8n workflow execution data.

Authentication: Bearer Token

Request Body: N8NWorkflowExecution

Response: N8NWebhookResponse

Status Codes: - 200 - Success - 401 - Unauthorized - 422 - Validation Error - 500 - Server Error

docs.title: GET /api/v1/webhooks/n8n/config
docs.text:
Get webhook configuration and setup instructions.

Authentication: Bearer Token

Response: N8NWorkflowConfig

Example: 

{
  "webhook_url": "https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/webhooks/n8n/execution",
  "track_all_nodes": true,
  "min_execution_time_ms": 0
}

docs.title: POST /api/v1/webhooks/n8n/test
docs.text:
Test webhook with sample data.

Authentication: Bearer Token

Response: 

{
  "status": "test_successful",
  "workflow_id": "uuid",
  "message": "Test webhook processed successfully"
}

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: All webhook requests require: - Valid Bearer token in Authorization header - Token associated with active organization - Proper permissions (webhooks:write)

docs.title: Data Privacy
docs.text:
• Webhook data is organization-scoped
  • Only users within the organization can view workflow data
  • Node input/output data is encrypted at rest
  • API keys never logged or stored in plaintext

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Webhook calls are authenticated by the API key in the Authorization header, like any other API request. An X-n8n-Signature header is accepted but not verified, so protect the key: store it in n8n credentials, use a dedicated key for n8n, and revoke it if the workflow is shared.

Webhook deliveries from n8n don't count as Governance Events.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Q: Can I use this with self-hosted n8n? A: Yes! The webhook integration works with both n8n Cloud and self-hosted instances.

Q: How much data can I send in a webhook? A: Maximum payload size is 10MB. For larger data, store in external storage and send references.

Q: Are webhooks processed synchronously? A: Yes, webhooks are processed immediately. Response typically within 100-500ms.

Q: Can I track multiple workflows? A: Yes, each workflow execution is tracked separately using unique execution_id.

Q: What happens if WhiteBoxXAI is down? A: n8n webhook will fail, but your workflow continues. Configure error handling to retry or log failures.

Q: Can I filter which nodes are tracked? A: Yes, modify the Code node to filter nodes before sending. You can also use min_execution_time_ms in config.

docs.title: Policy-as-Code & GitOps
docs.text: Keep your organization's model-release policy in the repository, next to the code it governs. A whitebox.yaml file says what should happen when a model has drifted or a bias audit has found bias. Your CI pipeline syncs it to WhiteBoxXAI and then asks, before a deployment, whether a model passes. Policy changes go through pull requests and review like any other change, and every evaluation says which rule caused a warning or a block.

docs.title: The policy file
docs.text:
# whitebox.yaml
minor_drift_action: warn      # when the model's latest drift report detected drift
major_bias_action: block      # when the model's latest bias audit detected bias
auto_approve_minor: false     # whether a clean evaluation is eligible for automatic approval
Key Checked against Values minor_drift_action The model's most recent drift report warn or block major_bias_action The model's most recent bias audit warn or block auto_approve_minor true or false
  • block fails the evaluation (allowed: false).
  • warn lets it pass, with the violation listed.
  • A key you leave out of your first sync starts at warn for drift and block for bias. On later syncs, a key you leave out keeps its current value.
  • A policy synced before validation was added may still hold agent_ticket or human_review. Both are evaluated as warn, so a violation is never silently passed.
  • The whole file is stored with the policy, other keys included, so you can see exactly what was synced.

docs.title: Sync the policy
docs.text:
Send the file's contents to WhiteBoxXAI. Run this on every merge to your main branch:

curl -X POST https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/policy/sync \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WHITEBOX_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "$(python -c 'import json,sys; print(json.dumps({"yaml_content": open("whitebox.yaml").read()}))')"

The sync is refused, and the policy in force stays unchanged, when:

  • the file isn't valid YAML, or isn't a mapping of keys to values: 400
  • an action is anything other than warn or block (including a different case, such as Block), or auto_approve_minor isn't true or false: 422, naming the key

GET /api/v1/policy returns the policy currently in force.

docs.title: Evaluate a model
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/policy/evaluate/<model-id> \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WHITEBOX_API_KEY"

{
  "model_id": "5d1c…",
  "policy_exists": true,
  "allowed": false,
  "action": "block",
  "auto_approve_eligible": false,
  "violations": [
    {"policy_rule": "minor_drift_action", "action": "warn", "detail": "Drift detected (score: 0.31)"},
    {"policy_rule": "major_bias_action", "action": "block", "detail": "Bias detected (overall fairness score: 0.62)"}
  ]
}
Field Meaning action pass, warn or block: the strictest action among the violations allowed false only when action is block violations Each rule that matched, its action, and the evidence behind it auto_approve_eligible true when nothing matched and auto_approve_minor is on policy_exists false if no policy has been synced; the evaluation then passes

The evaluation reads the model's latest drift report and bias audit. Create a fresh drift report and run a bias audit in the pipeline first if you want the decision based on the build you're about to deploy. Neither is created by the evaluation itself.

docs.title: Gate a deployment in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
The WhiteBoxXAI Governance Action runs the sync and the evaluation in one step, and fails the job on block:

# .github/workflows/governance.yml
name: Model governance
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  policy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: AgentaFlow/whitebox-governance-action@v1
        with:
          api_key: ${{ secrets.WHITEBOX_API_KEY }}
          model_id: ${{ vars.WHITEBOX_MODEL_ID }}
          # Sync only on main, so a pull request can't change the policy in force.
          sync: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' }}

On a pull request, the step evaluates the model against the policy already in force. After the merge to main, it syncs the reviewed file first.

Input Default Description api_key (required) A WhiteBoxXAI API key. Store it as a repository secret, never in the workflow file. policy_file whitebox.yaml Path to the policy file. sync true Sync the policy file before evaluating. model_id The model to evaluate. Leave it empty to sync only. base_url WHITEBOX_BASE_URL, then https://api.whiteboxxai.com The API address. On Business Cloud, set it to your tenant's API address. Output Description action pass, warn or block allowed false only when action is block violations The violations as a JSON array

Each violation appears as an annotation on the run: a warning for warn, an error for block. The step also fails on any error from the API, such as a bad key, an unknown model, or a policy file that's refused. To fail on a warning too, give the step an id and check its output:

      - uses: AgentaFlow/whitebox-governance-action@v1
        id: policy
        with:
          api_key: ${{ secrets.WHITEBOX_API_KEY }}
          model_id: ${{ vars.WHITEBOX_MODEL_ID }}
      - if: steps.policy.outputs.action == 'warn'
        run: exit 1

The Action runs in a Docker container, so it needs a Linux runner. On other runners or CI systems, call the two endpoints above directly and fail the job when action is block.

docs.title: What it gives an auditor
docs.text:
• The policy is versioned in Git: who changed it, when, and through which reviewed pull request.
  • Each evaluation names the rule, the action and the evidence (the drift or bias result) behind a warning or block.
  • The drift reports and bias audits the evaluation relied on are stored in WhiteBoxXAI with ids you can cite, and appear in the Model Register dossier.

For approvals that need people rather than a pipeline, route the change through Reviews & Decisions.

docs.title: TensorFlow & Keras
docs.text: Examples use feature_names for your model's input feature names. Every registration sends a valid model_type (neural_network for Keras models), a version, features and baseline_metrics, which the API requires.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install whitebox-xai-sdk[tensorflow]

docs.title: Basic Setup
docs.text:
import os
from tensorflow import keras
from whiteboxxai import WhiteBoxXAI
from whiteboxxai.integrations.tensorflow import KerasMonitor, WhiteBoxXAICallback

# Initialize client
client = WhiteBoxXAI(api_key=os.environ["WHITEBOX_API_KEY"])

# Create monitor
monitor = KerasMonitor(
    client=client,
    model=your_model,
    model_name="my_keras_model",
    model_type="neural_network",
)

# Register model
model_id = monitor.register_from_model(
    version="1.0.0",
    features=feature_names,
    baseline_metrics={},      # add metrics you measured on your test set
)

docs.title: Training with Monitoring
docs.text:
# Create callback
callback = WhiteBoxXAICallback(
    monitor=monitor,
    log_frequency=1,  # Log every epoch
    log_validation=True
)

# Train
model.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    validation_split=0.2,
    callbacks=[callback],
    epochs=50
)

docs.title: Making Predictions
docs.text:
# With automatic logging
predictions = monitor.predict(X_test, log=True)

# With actual values
predictions = monitor.predict(X_test, log=True, actuals=y_test)

# Without logging
predictions = monitor.predict(X_test, log=False)

docs.title: Baseline for Drift Detection
docs.text: monitor.set_baseline(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: Wrapping Existing Models
docs.text:
from whiteboxxai.integrations.tensorflow import wrap_keras_model

# Wrap model for automatic logging
wrapped_model = wrap_keras_model(model, monitor)

# All predictions now automatically logged
predictions = wrapped_model.predict(X_test)

docs.title: Logging Metrics
docs.text:
# Log epoch metrics
monitor.log_epoch(
    epoch=10,
    train_loss=0.5,
    val_loss=0.6,
    accuracy=0.85
)

# Log checkpoint
monitor.log_checkpoint(
    epoch=10,
    checkpoint_path="checkpoints/model_10.h5",
    metrics={'accuracy': 0.9}
)

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
import os
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from tensorflow import keras
from whiteboxxai import WhiteBoxXAI
from whiteboxxai.integrations.tensorflow import KerasMonitor, WhiteBoxXAICallback

# Generate data
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=1000, n_features=20, random_state=42)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)

# Standardize
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test = scaler.transform(X_test)

# Build model
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu', input_shape=(20,)),
    keras.layers.Dropout(0.3),
    keras.layers.Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    keras.layers.Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
])

model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

# Setup monitoring
client = WhiteBoxXAI(api_key=os.environ["WHITEBOX_API_KEY"])
monitor = KerasMonitor(client, model=model, model_name="demo_model", model_type="neural_network")
monitor.register_from_model(
    version="1.0.0",
    features=[f"x{i}" for i in range(20)],
    baseline_metrics={},
)
monitor.set_baseline(X_train, y_train)

# Train with monitoring
callback = WhiteBoxXAICallback(monitor)
model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_split=0.2,
          callbacks=[callback], epochs=50)

# Predict and log
predictions = monitor.predict(X_test, log=True, actuals=y_test)

print(f"Model registered with ID: {monitor.model_id}")

docs.title: Custom Metrics Callback
docs.text:
class MetricsCallback(keras.callbacks.Callback):
    def __init__(self, monitor):
        self.monitor = monitor

    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
        lr = float(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(self.model.optimizer.learning_rate))
        self.monitor.log_epoch(epoch=epoch, learning_rate=lr, **logs)

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always set baseline before production deployment
  2. Use callbacks during training for automatic logging
  3. Log validation data to track model performance
  4. Save checkpoints at regular intervals
  5. Version your models using the version parameter
  6. Use descriptive names for easy identification
  7. Monitor GPU memory in production
  8. Enable async logging for high-throughput scenarios
