docs.text:
from whiteboxxai.offline import OfflineManager

manager = OfflineManager(
    offline_dir="./queue",
    max_queue_size=10000,
    auto_sync=True,
    sync_interval=60,
    max_retries=3
)

manager.set_client(client)
"""Set WhiteBoxXAI client for syncing."""

manager.start_auto_sync()
"""Start background sync thread."""

manager.stop_auto_sync()
"""Stop background sync thread."""

manager.sync(batch_size=100) -> Dict[str, int]
"""Manually sync queued operations."""

manager.get_status() -> Dict[str, Any]
"""Get status and statistics."""

manager.cleanup(older_than_days: int = 7)
"""Remove old completed operations."""

manager.queue
"""The underlying OfflineQueue instance."""

docs.text:
See offline_mode_example.py in the public SDK repository for complete examples:

  1. Basic offline mode with auto-sync
  2. Manual sync control

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Enable for Production: Always use offline mode in production
  2. Monitor Queue Size: Set up alerts for large queues
  3. Regular Cleanup: Clean old operations to prevent disk bloat
  4. Persistent Location: Use /var/lib or similar for queue storage
  5. Error Monitoring: Track failed operations and investigate patterns — requeue_failed() only helps once you've fixed the cause
  6. Test Offline Scenarios: Verify behavior when API is unavailable
  7. Context Managers: Use with statement for proper cleanup
  8. Upgrade to 1.0.0+: Earlier versions queued nothing and could not sync

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The offline queue stores operation data in SQLite:

  • Database file location: {offline_dir}/queue.db
  • Contains API call data (inputs, outputs, metadata)
  • Ensure appropriate file permissions in production
  • Consider encryption for sensitive data directories
# Set appropriate permissions
chmod 700 /var/lib/whiteboxxai/queue

docs.title: The Enhanced Dashboard
docs.text:
The Enhanced Dashboard is organized around the questions a risk or compliance team gets asked: Where do our AI systems stand? What needs a decision? What would we hand an auditor today? Each section answers one of them, and every number it shows comes with a How was this computed? note that says exactly what data produced it.

It's the default layout for every account. This page explains how it's laid out; the pages under Enhanced Dashboard in the navigation cover each section in depth.

docs.title: The sidebar
docs.text:
Group Section Use it to Guide Focus Overview See where your AI systems stand, run the readiness setup, present to a board Overview Needs Attention Work through alerts, risks, reviews and deadlines, worst first Needs Attention AI Systems Model Register Browse every governed AI system and open its dossier Model Register Assurance Explainability, fairness and drift for a system, each with a verdict Assurance Observability Runtime performance, LLM & RAG activity, agents and prompt evaluations Observability, Evaluations Evidence & Governance Compliance & Evidence Frameworks, controls, evidence, reports, the calendar and the audit trail Compliance & Evidence, Reports Reviews & Decisions Review requests, board votes, the decision archive and RACI Reviews & Decisions Risk Register AI risks scored by likelihood and impact AI Risk Register

Badges on the sidebar count what's waiting: the Needs Attention queue total, your pending reviews, and open risks. The footer links to these docs, Support and Settings.

The header shows your organization, when the data was last refreshed, Search ⌘K, a theme toggle, and a bell that opens Needs Attention with the number of active alerts. When sample data is loaded, a Demo data — illustrative only label appears so nobody mistakes it for your own.

docs.title: Lenses: "View as"
docs.text:
Different people read the same evidence differently. The View as menu switches the lens:

  • Compliance Officer
  • Data Scientist
  • Executive
  • Auditor
  • Admin (administrators only)

A lens "changes which columns and wording lead. It never changes what you can do." For example, the Data Scientist lens leads the Model Register with drift and fairness-gap columns, the Compliance Officer lens with risk tier, evidence and attestation, and the Executive lens opens the Overview on Value & impact. Your role, not your lens, decides what you're allowed to do.

The lens also shapes report wording: see Settings → Writing style.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role Can Administrator Everything, including users, API keys, framework adoption, control decisions, evidence approval, board setup and scales Analyst Work with systems and evidence, mark verdicts reviewed, file evidence, and propose readiness changes for an administrator to confirm Viewer Read everything they have access to

Some actions depend on more than your role. You can't vote on a review request you raised, and voting needs two-factor authentication and an authenticator code. See Reviews & Decisions.

docs.title: Search and commands (⌘K)
docs.text:
Press ⌘K (macOS) or Ctrl+K (Windows, Linux) to open Quick Actions. Type to search:

  • Systems, controls, generated reports and review requests, by name
  • Commands, such as Generate board pack, Open framework gaps for each framework, or Take the product tour
  • Create entries: register a model, create an alert rule, generate a report
  • Navigation and Settings & Help

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text: Keys Action g then o Go to Overview g then a Go to Needs Attention g then r Go to Model Register g then e Go to Compliance & Evidence g then v Go to Reviews & Decisions ⌘K / Ctrl+K Search and run commands ? Show the keyboard shortcuts list

docs.title: Saved views
docs.text:
On the Model Register and the Needs Attention queue, set the filters and columns you want and choose Saved views → Save current view.... Saved views are:

  • private to you
  • kept per lens, so your Auditor views and Data Scientist views stay separate
  • synced across your browsers
  • limited to 25 per account across all screens

docs.title: "How was this computed?"
docs.text: Every tile, verdict and chart that summarises your data has a How was this computed? control. It says which records were counted, over what period, and with what method. When there isn't enough data, the dashboard says Not instrumented, Not available or Assessment not started instead of showing a number. WhiteBoxXAI never fills a gap with an estimate.

docs.title: Product tour
docs.text: The product tour walks through Overview, Needs Attention, Model Register, Assurance, Observability, Compliance & Evidence, Reviews & Decisions, and search and shortcuts. Start it from ⌘K → Take the product tour or Settings → Sample data & tour.

docs.title: Enhanced and Classic layouts
docs.text:
The Classic layout, the dashboard before the Enhanced redesign, remains available for now.

  • Switch to Classic: avatar menu → Switch to Classic layout, or Settings → Preferences → Layout → Classic layout.
  • Switch to Enhanced: the Try the new layout button in the Classic header (shown on wider screens), or Settings → Preferences → Layout → New layout.

Your choice syncs to your account. Links to Classic pages open the matching Enhanced section or tab when you're on the Enhanced layout, so bookmarks keep working.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text: Settings → Preferences sets your layout, default lens, theme (Light, Dark or Match my device) and density (Comfortable or Compact). See Settings for every pane.

docs.title: Assurance
docs.text:
An auditor's next questions after what AI do you run are why did it decide that, is it fair, and is it still behaving the way it did when you approved it. Assurance answers those three for one system, or for all of them, "in the language your auditor will accept".

Every result is computed from the predictions you logged, not from a template. Each tab leads with a plain-language verdict, has a How was this computed? note, and lets analysts and administrators Mark reviewed. With too little data, the tab says the result can't be computed yet rather than estimating one.

Use Choose a system (or All systems) at the top. The tabs are Explainability, Fairness and Drift.

docs.title: Explainability
docs.text:
Explanations run your model

SHAP, LIME and DiCE explanations are computed by running the model itself, so WhiteBoxXAI needs the model file. Register the model through GitHub with storage_mode: full; scikit-learn-style pickle and joblib files are supported. For a model registered with metadata only, the explanation is recorded as failed, with a message saying no stored model artifact is available. Drift, fairness audits and reports don't need the model file.

docs.title: Request an explanation
docs.text:
1. Choose a system, then a logged prediction to explain.

  2. Pick a Method:

    Method Use it for Model default The method configured for this system SHAP (kernel) Any model; model-agnostic Shapley values SHAP (tree models) Tree ensembles such as XGBoost, LightGBM and random forests; exact and fast LIME (tabular) A local linear approximation around the prediction DiCE (counterfactuals) What would have to change for a different outcome?

  3. Request the explanation. Results appear when the computation finishes.

docs.title: Read the result
docs.text:
• Contribution waterfall: how each feature moved the prediction away from the base value
  • Force plot: the features pushing the prediction up and down, side by side
  • Feature weights: the ranked contributions
  • What this explanation shows: a plain-language reading of the result

Counterfactuals (DiCE) answer the question an applicant or customer actually asks: what would have needed to be different? Each counterfactual is an alternative input, close to the original, that the model scores differently. From the SDK you can choose how many to generate (total_cfs, default 3), the target outcome (desired_class, default "opposite") and which features may change (features_to_vary, default "all"). Restrict features_to_vary to features a person could realistically change. Counterfactuals that vary age or protected attributes aren't useful recourse.

cf = client.explanations.generate(
    model_id,
    instance={"income": 52000, "utilisation": 0.31, "tenure_months": 18},
    method="dice",
    total_cfs=3,
    features_to_vary=["income", "utilisation"],
)

For how SHAP and LIME values are computed, and global feature importance, see Explainability Engine.

docs.title: Fairness
docs.text:
Choose a Protected attribute (All, Gender, Race/Ethnicity, Age, Disability), then read the sub-tabs:

Sub-tab Shows Fairness Metrics Demographic parity, equalized odds, disparate impact and the other metrics computed by the audit Group Comparison Outcomes and error rates per group, side by side Audit Results Each recorded audit, its severity, and whether it passed Recommendations The mitigations the audit recorded for this result

docs.title: Where audit data comes from
docs.text:
A fairness audit needs true outcomes, predicted outcomes and group membership. WhiteBoxXAI doesn't infer protected attributes from other columns. You supply group data you're entitled to use when you run the audit:

audit = client.fairness.audit(
    model_id,
    sensitive_attributes=["gender"],
    y_true=y_true,
    y_pred=y_pred,
    group_data={"gender": genders},
)

If you don't have that data, the audit can't be run, and the tab says so. A failed audit with high severity can draft an entry in the AI Risk Register automatically.

For the metric definitions and thresholds, see Bias Detection.

docs.title: Drift
docs.text:
Choose a drift type and a time range, then read the sub-tabs:

Sub-tab Shows Overview The verdict and overall drift score for the period Feature Analysis Per-feature test results and which features drifted Timeline How drift has changed over time Details The test statistics behind each result

Refresh re-reads the latest results. Export Report downloads the drift results as CSV, and every chart can also be exported as PNG or CSV.

docs.title: How drift is measured
docs.text:
Each feature in a recent window of predictions is compared with the model's baseline:

  • Continuous features: Kolmogorov–Smirnov test and Population Stability Index (PSI)
  • Categorical features: chi-squared test and Jensen–Shannon divergence
  • Concept drift: performance degradation against the baseline, and distribution-based methods including ADWIN

Sensitivity presets (low, medium, high) set all the thresholds together. See Drift Detection for configuration.

docs.title: Keep a record
docs.text:
A quick check (client.drift.detect) answers has it drifted? without storing anything. A drift report (client.drift.create_report) is stored with an id you can cite, appears in the Model Register dossier, and can be turned into a Drift Report document in Reports. Use reports for anything you'll show someone else.

High-severity drift can draft an entry in the AI Risk Register automatically.

docs.title: Who can do what
docs.text:
Action Who View results and verdicts Everyone in the organization Mark reviewed on a verdict Analysts and administrators

Requesting an explanation, running a fairness audit or creating a drift report from the SDK, REST API or MCP server records one Governance Event. Doing it from the dashboard is free.

docs.title: Compliance & Evidence
docs.text:
Compliance & Evidence shows what an auditor would be handed today, and exactly which controls would still be missing an artifact. It works across the five frameworks WhiteBoxXAI covers: ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, GDPR, CCPA and NIST AI RMF.

WhiteBoxXAI records evidence; it does not certify compliance. It shows which controls you've decided apply, which have approved evidence, and where the gaps are. Whether that evidence satisfies a regulator or auditor is your organization's call.

Press g then e to get here. The tabs are Frameworks, Controls, Evidence packs, Reports, Calendar and Audit trail.

docs.title: Frameworks
docs.text:
One card per framework. Each card shows:

  • N of M controls with approved evidence: always a count, never a percentage
  • Not adopted, Assessment not started or Start assessment when there's nothing to count yet
  • the next audit date
  • up to three open gaps, each with an action to close it, such as File evidence, Run a fairness audit, Generate a model card, Update the risk register, Review monitoring, Review open alerts, Review consent records or Upload the policy document

Adopting a framework and setting its audit date are part of the readiness setup.

docs.title: Framework detail
docs.text:
Open the framework opens a detail panel with framework-specific records:

Framework Detail panel ISO/IEC 42001 Controls by clause (4–10), open gaps, assessments recorded, Record an assessment, Download the certification package (JSON). AIMS Policies & Guidelines, with an Approve step for policies pending approval, and AI Objectives. EU AI Act Assessments against the EU AI Act, risk classification per system, and conformity assessments GDPR Data subject requests (newest first) and the breach register CCPA Consumer requests NIST AI RMF Categories by core function (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) with open risks per function, open gaps and assessments recorded

docs.title: ISO/IEC 42001 policies and objectives
docs.text:
The ISO/IEC 42001 panel has registers for AIMS Policies & Guidelines (Clause 5) and AI Objectives (Clause 6.2):

  1. Record AIMS Policy: give the policy a title (for example Organizational AI Acceptable Use Policy), a Version and its Content: the policy statements, scope and operational requirements. A new policy is Pending Approval.
  2. Approve: an administrator approves a pending policy, and it shows as Approved. The approval is recorded in the audit trail with the approver's name.
  3. Add AI Objective: an Objective Title (for example Maintain demographic disparity under 5%), a Description & Criteria with measurable targets, verification cadence and responsible roles, and a Target Date.

Approved policies and recorded objectives are evidence for the ISO/IEC 42001 leadership and planning clauses.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
The Controls tab lists every control for a framework, with Gaps, Undecided and Excluded filters and a search box (Search refs or titles).

Column Meaning Control The control's reference and title Applies? Your applicability decision Status Evidenced, Gap or Excluded Evidence Evidence filed against the control Justification Why a control was excluded

docs.title: Decide applicability (administrators)
docs.text: Decide (or Change decision) records whether a control applies to you. Excluding a control requires a written justification, which appears in the Statement of Applicability and other reports. Mandatory controls are marked Always applies and can't be excluded. Administrators can also Add a custom control for an internal requirement, and Deactivate one later.

docs.title: File evidence
docs.text:
File evidence uploads an artifact against a control. Artifact types include bias audit report, impact assessment, model card, risk assessment, data lineage documentation, audit report, policy document, training record, vendor assessment, monitoring report, incident report and consent record.

New evidence is pending until an administrator approves it: "An administrator approves it before it counts." Only approved evidence counts towards a framework's "N of M".

docs.title: Evidence by artifact
docs.text: One artifact often satisfies controls in several frameworks: a bias audit report maps to controls in all five. Evidence by artifact shows that crosswalk, so you file once and see every control it supports.

docs.title: Collect system evidence
docs.text: Collect system evidence gathers evidence WhiteBoxXAI already holds and files it for review: bias audits, drift reports, model cards, access reviews and CI/CD lineage. Collected items are filed as pending, so an administrator still decides what counts.

docs.title: ServiceNow AI Control Tower
docs.text:
If your change approvals, vendor risk assessments and AI governance records live in ServiceNow AI Control Tower, you shouldn't have to retype them as evidence. WhiteBoxXAI pulls them in as the technical evidence behind them.

An administrator turns on the ServiceNow AI Control Tower integration first (it appears as a status card under Settings → Integrations). Then Sync from ServiceNow AICT, in Evidence by artifact, reads records from your instance. It reads the change_request table by default, up to 50 records at a time (500 at most), and can take a ServiceNow query to narrow them. The tables it accepts are:

  • sn_ai_governance_asset_governance_details, cmdb_ci_appl_ai_application, cmdb_ci_function_ai and alm_ai_dataset_digital_asset
  • sn_vdr_risk_asmt_assessment (vendor risk assessments)
  • change_request (change approvals) and incident
  • sn_compliance_policy_exception and sn_risk_risk

What happens to each record:

  1. It is stored as an exact JSON snapshot with a SHA-256 hash. A record that hasn't changed since the last sync is skipped, so syncing twice doesn't file it twice ("N new evidence artifacts created, M unchanged records skipped").
  2. It is filed as pending. Like every other evidence item, it doesn't count towards a framework until an administrator approves it, because a ServiceNow ticket existing isn't the same as the control being met.

Records can also be pushed to WhiteBoxXAI instead of pulled. Send them to POST /api/v1/integrations/servicenow/evidence, or point a ServiceNow business rule at POST /api/v1/integrations/servicenow/webhook, which does the same thing. Both use your normal API key or session. See the REST API Reference.

docs.title: Evidence packs
docs.text:
Compose a pack for one AI system or the whole organization, as PDF or HTML, and click Generate evidence pack. The pack is saved to Reports → History, where it can be signed off and shared with an auditor.

Choose the Reporting period: Last 30 days, Last 90 days or Last 12 months. The trust score and the risk register show their state when the pack is generated; the other sections cover the period you chose.

What's in this pack previews the contents before you generate, and changes with your choice:

  • Always included: a cover with the scope, the period and how many findings sit at each rating; for each section, what it shows an auditor and which requirements it is relevant to; and charts where there is enough data to draw one, with missing data named as missing.
  • Organization-wide: every finding with its rating, the trust score across all AI systems, open high and critical risks from the register, and the audit trail for the period.
  • Added when you pick one AI system: performance against the baseline, data and concept drift, bias and fairness audits, and explainability coverage.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: The Reports tab is the Report Studio: 12 report types, templates, branding, history with sign-off, auditor share links and schedules. See Reports.

docs.title: Calendar
docs.text:
A month view with Today and previous/next navigation, plus an Agenda: Overdue, Next 90 days, Later, Regulatory dates already past and Completed.

Item Comes from Audit Audit dates you set for each framework Questionnaire, Internal Milestones an administrator adds Regulatory date Regulatory milestones, each with its citation and the date it was last checked Review due Scheduled governance reviews Risk treatment due Treatment due dates from the AI Risk Register

Administrators can add, edit, complete, reopen and delete milestones. Deadlines within your chosen window also appear in Needs Attention.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
Every recorded action, by whom and when, for a period from 24 hours to 90 days:

  • Integrity check: N of M events verified. Each event is chained to the previous one, so an altered or deleted event shows up as unverified.
  • Compliance report: download the period's audit trail as PDF or CSV
  • Panels: Events in this period; events by category, severity and outcome; Most active; Events over time; and the Events list with filters, search and paging
  • Retention: how long audit events are kept

docs.title: From code
docs.text:
client.compliance.list_frameworks()
client.compliance.get_framework_controls("eu_ai_act")       # a key from list_frameworks()
client.compliance.iso42001_score()
client.compliance.iso42001_gaps(severity_filter="high")

Unassessed controls come back marked as not assessed. Report them that way, never as a likely pass. See Compliance frameworks for what WhiteBoxXAI records for each framework.

docs.title: Evaluations & Prompt Versions
docs.text:
A prompt change can quietly make an LLM application worse, and a regulator or customer can ask you to show it didn't. Observability → Evaluations gives you the evidence: golden datasets of expected behaviour, scored runs against a specific prompt version, and a regression check between two runs. Prompts are versioned and governed like models.

Deterministic scoring, no LLM-as-a-judge

Evaluations score outputs your model already produced, stored with each dataset row or reported by your own test pipeline. Every score comes from a deterministic, repeatable check (exact match, required phrases or rule-based rubric checks) that an auditor can re-run and get the same answer. WhiteBoxXAI never sends prompts to your model or to any third-party LLM on your behalf, and never asks another model to judge or grade results.

The tab has three parts: Runs, Golden datasets and Prompts.

docs.title: Golden datasets
docs.text:
A golden dataset is "a set of inputs with the output you expect for each."

  1. New dataset: give it a name and, optionally, what it's for.
  2. Add a row for each case:
    • Input (JSON object): what was sent to the model
    • Expected output (JSON object, optional): what a correct answer looks like
    • Stored model output (JSON object, optional): "The output your model gave for this input. A run scores this; without it the row is not evaluated."

Rows without a stored output are shown as Not evaluated in every run. They're never counted as passes.

docs.title: Score a prompt version
docs.text:
Score a prompt version creates an evaluation run for one prompt version against one golden dataset. Choose How to score:

Method What it checks Exact match "Compare each stored output with the row's expected output." Required phrases "Check each stored output for the phrases in the row's must_contain list." Rule-based checks "Compare expected values, and apply the no-PII rule if the rubric names it." You can add a rubric and the score a row must reach to pass (0 to 1). Scored by your pipeline Results your own test pipeline or the SDK reported. "WhiteBox recorded them as sent."

Results read as N of M evaluated rows passed, with Not evaluated rows listed separately. Every run records How it was scored. A run that didn't record its method says so rather than guessing.

Each evaluation run started through the API counts as one Governance Event. Authoring datasets and prompts is free.

docs.title: Check a prompt change for regressions
docs.text:
Check a prompt change for regressions compares two runs on the same dataset:

  • Baseline run: the version in use
  • Candidate run: the change

The result is one of three verdicts:

  • No regression found
  • Regression found, with the Cases that got worse
  • Cannot tell, for example when too few rows were judged in both runs

The comparison lists rows that Got better, Got worse or stayed Unchanged, and which were Left out because they weren't judged in one or both runs. Both runs must use the same dataset.

docs.title: Prompt versions
docs.text:
Under Prompts, New prompt creates a prompt template. Open it to see its versions, newest first, and Save a new version. A version records:

  • User message and System message
  • Target model and Temperature setting
  • Git commit: the code it shipped with
  • Tool schemas
  • Version tag

Versions can't be edited or deleted. A change is always a new version, so the history is complete.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Each version moves through a governed lifecycle:

design → verify → deploy → retired

The Lifecycle Stage badge shows where a version is. Verified (Benchmark Verification) shows that it passed verification, and Active marks the version in use. A version can't be deployed without a passed verification. If a deployed version misbehaves, roll back to an earlier one, with a recorded reason.

Lifecycle changes, deployment and rollback are done from the SDK or MCP server:

v = client.prompts.create_version(template_id, user_message_template="...", version_tag="v3")
client.prompts.advance_stage(template_id, v["id"], target_stage="verify")
client.prompts.deploy(template_id, v["id"])          # refused without a passed verification
client.prompts.rollback(template_id, target_version_id=previous_id, reason="tone regression")

docs.title: Link calls to a version
docs.text:
Pass prompt_version_id when you log LLM calls. Every call in the LLM & RAG audit trail is then attributable to the exact prompt that produced it, and prompt drift reports and incidents can be traced to a version:

client.llm.log_call(
    provider="openai",
    model_name="gpt-4o",
    prompt=rendered_prompt,
    completion=answer,
    latency_ms=640.0,
    prompt_version_id=active_version_id,
)

See LLM monitoring and the prompts tools on the MCP Server.

docs.title: Model Registry
docs.text: The Model Registry is your central hub for managing all ML models.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: - Centralize model information - Track model versions - Monitor model lifecycle - Document model metadata

Key Capabilities: - Register unlimited models (plan-dependent) - Version tracking by name - Tags and metadata - Model archival

docs.title: Via Web UI
docs.text:
1. Go to Model Register and click Register a system.

  2. Fill in the form:

    Basic Information

    • Model Name (required): a descriptive name, such as "Credit Risk Predictor"
    • Version: for example 1.0.0
    • Description: what the model does and its intended use
    • Model Type (required): Binary Classification, Multi-class Classification, Regression, Time Series, Clustering or Other. Recorded as a tag.
    • Architecture (required): XGBoost, Random Forest, Neural Network, Linear Model, LLM or Custom
    • Framework (required): Scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, XGBoost, LightGBM, Keras or Other
    • Tags: for example production, finance

    Model Metadata

    • Target Variable and Feature List (comma-separated)
    • Baseline Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and AUC-ROC from your own test evaluation. Leave blank any you didn't measure.

  3. Click Register Model.

docs.title: Via SDK
docs.text:
from whiteboxxai import WhiteBoxXAI

client = WhiteBoxXAI()

model = client.models.register(
    name="Customer Churn Predictor",
    model_type="xgboost",
    version="2.1.0",
    framework="xgboost",
    description="Predicts customer churn risk using behavioral data",
    features=[
        "account_age_days",
        "total_purchases",
        "avg_purchase_value",
        "days_since_last_purchase",
        "customer_service_calls",
        "satisfaction_score"
    ],
    target_variable="will_churn",
    baseline_metrics={
        "accuracy": 0.89,
        "precision": 0.85,
        "recall": 0.82,
        "f1_score": 0.835,
        "auc_roc": 0.93
    },
    tags=["production", "customer-retention", "high-priority"],
)

print(f"Model registered with ID: {model['id']}")

Every SDK call returns a plain dict

Not an object with attributes. It's model["id"], not model.id, throughout this page — that applies to every SDK response shown below, not just this one.

There's also auto_detect_git=True, which reads the current commit, branch, and working-tree state from the repository you're registering from and attaches them automatically — the Git-side half of the traceability GitHub Integration provides. Add require_clean_git=True to refuse registration with uncommitted changes.

docs.title: Via REST API
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WHITEBOX_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "Customer Churn Predictor",
    "version": "2.1.0",
    "model_type": "xgboost",
    "features": ["account_age_days", "total_purchases"],
    "baseline_metrics": {"accuracy": 0.89}
  }'

model_type must be one of xgboost, random_forest, neural_network, linear_model, llm or custom. A task name such as classification is rejected; pick the family closest to your model, or custom.

docs.title: Model Versioning
docs.text:
Version is a free-text string you choose — semantic versioning (2.1.0) is a sane convention, not something the platform enforces. Register a new version under the same name to track it as part of that model's history:

# Register a new version under the same name
client.models.register(
    name="Customer Churn Predictor",
    model_type="custom",
    version="2.2.0",
    features=feature_names,
    baseline_metrics={"accuracy": 0.91},
)

# List every version registered under that name, newest first
versions = client.models.get_versions(model_name="Customer Churn Predictor")
for v in versions:
    print(f"v{v['version']} - {v['status']} - {v['created_at']}")

# Or just the most recent one
latest = client.models.get_latest(model_name="Customer Churn Predictor")

To compare the model files behind two versions (layers, parameters, hyperparameters, shapes), use model-diff reviews on Git-backed versions: client.models.list_git_versions(model_id), then client.models.compare_versions(version1_id, version2_id), or open Lineage & versions in the system's dossier in the Model Register. See GitHub Diff Reviews.

docs.title: Model Metadata
docs.text:
Tracked Automatically: - Registration date - Last updated - Prediction count - Last prediction timestamp - Active alerts - Drift status

Update model fields:

update() is a partial update — only the fields you pass change. The full field list is description, status, features, baseline_metrics, target_variable, model_framework, fairness_attributes, protected_groups, and tags; there's no free-form metadata dict beyond those.

client.models.update(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    description="Retrained on Q4 data; approved by risk committee 2026-08-20.",
    tags=["production", "compliance-approved"],
)

If you need to track something not on that list — an owner, a model card URL, a risk rating — put it in your own system of record, or as free text in description, or as a custom metric if it's numeric and you want it on the dashboard.

docs.title: Model Status Lifecycle
docs.text:
Statuses: active, deprecated, archived. There's no separate "draft" or "staging" status — a model is either active and monitored, or it isn't.

# Update status
client.models.update_status(model_id="model-uuid", new_status="deprecated")

# Archive a model (soft delete — data is preserved, monitoring stops)
client.models.archive(model_id="old-model-uuid")

# Bring it back
client.models.restore(model_id="old-model-uuid")

docs.title: Model Organization
docs.text:
Tags: 

# Set (replaces the existing tag list)
client.models.update(model_id="model-uuid", tags=["production", "high-priority"])

# Search by tags
prod_models = client.models.list(tags=["production"])

docs.title: Prediction Logging
docs.text: Track all model predictions for monitoring and analysis.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: - Monitor prediction patterns - Calculate performance metrics - Detect drift - Enable explainability - Audit trail for compliance

What to Log: - Input features (input_data) - Model output — prediction, probability, whatever your model returns (output_data) - Metadata (optional)

No ground-truth label update yet

There's no endpoint today for attaching an actual outcome to a prediction after the fact (a "here's what really happened" update). Accuracy and other metrics that need ground truth work from data you log yourself, joined outside the platform, until that ships.

docs.title: 1. Manual Logging
docs.text:
Log individual predictions explicitly:

from whiteboxxai import WhiteBoxXAI

client = WhiteBoxXAI()

# After your model predicts
features = {
    "age": 35,
    "income": 75000,
    "credit_score": 720,
    "debt_ratio": 0.35
}

prediction = model.predict([list(features.values())])[0]
probability = model.predict_proba([list(features.values())])[0][1]

# Log to WhiteBoxXAI
response = client.predictions.log(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    input_data=features,
    output_data={
        "prediction": int(prediction),
        "probability": float(probability)
    },
    metadata={
        "customer_id": "CUST-12345",
        "application_id": "APP-67890",
        "channel": "web"
    }
)

print(f"Logged: {response['prediction_id']}")

docs.title: 2. ModelMonitor — the higher-level path
docs.text:
For most integrations, ModelMonitor is less code than calling client.predictions.log() directly — it holds the model ID, and adds optional local buffering and sampling. See SDK Documentation for the full API.

from whiteboxxai import WhiteBoxXAI, ModelMonitor

client = WhiteBoxXAI()
monitor = ModelMonitor(client, model_id="model-uuid")

prediction = model.predict([list(features.values())])[0]
probability = model.predict_proba([list(features.values())])[0][1]

monitor.log_prediction(
    inputs=features,
    output={"prediction": int(prediction), "probability": float(probability)},
)

Wrap it in a decorator with monitor_model() if you'd rather not touch the call site at all:

from whiteboxxai.decorators import monitor_model

@monitor_model(monitor, input_keys=["features"])
def predict_loan_approval(features):
    prediction = model.predict([features])[0]
    probability = model.predict_proba([features])[0][1]
    return {"prediction": int(prediction), "probability": float(probability)}

# Logging happens automatically on every call
result = predict_loan_approval(features=[35, 75000, 720, 0.35])

docs.title: 3. Batch Logging
docs.text:
Log multiple predictions in one call — each item needs input_data/output_data, matching the single-prediction shape:

predictions = []

for customer in customers:
    features = extract_features(customer)
    pred = model.predict([features])
    prob = model.predict_proba([features])[0][1]

    predictions.append({
        "input_data": features,
        "output_data": {
            "prediction": int(pred[0]),
            "probability": float(prob)
        },
        "metadata": {"customer_id": customer.id}
    })

# Log batch (up to 1,000 per call)
response = client.predictions.log_batch(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    predictions=predictions
)

print(f"Logged {response['logged']} of {response['total']} ({response['failed']} failed)")

docs.title: 4. Framework Integration
docs.text:
Scikit-learn: 

from whiteboxxai.integrations.sklearn import SklearnMonitor

sklearn_monitor = SklearnMonitor(client=client, model=my_sklearn_model, model_id="model-uuid")
monitored_model = sklearn_monitor.wrap_model(my_sklearn_model)

# Use like normal — logging is automatic
predictions = monitored_model.predict(X_test)
probabilities = monitored_model.predict_proba(X_test)

PyTorch: 

from whiteboxxai.integrations.pytorch import TorchMonitor

torch_monitor = TorchMonitor(client=client, model=pytorch_model)
monitored_model = torch_monitor.wrap_model(pytorch_model)

outputs = monitored_model(inputs)  # Forward pass logs automatically

See SDK Documentation for register_from_model(model_type="neural_network", version="1.0.0", features=feature_names, baseline_metrics={}, ) and the full framework-integration reference.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
Set sampling_rate on the monitor rather than on the model — it's a client-side decision about how much of your own traffic to send, not a server-side model setting:

# Log 10% of predictions, chosen randomly
monitor = ModelMonitor(client, model_id="model-uuid", sampling_rate=0.1)

For anything more targeted than uniform random sampling — stratified by confidence, higher during business hours, always log the ones you'd actually want to review — decide in your own code whether to call log_prediction() for a given prediction; there's no server-side stratified-sampling config to configure instead.

# Example: always log low-confidence predictions, sample the rest
if probability > 0.9 or probability < 0.1:
    should_log = True
else:
    should_log = random.random() < 0.05

if should_log:
    monitor.log_prediction(inputs=features, output=output)

Recommendations: - < 1k/day: 100% (log all) - 1k-10k/day: 10-50% - 10k-100k/day: 1-10% - > 100k/day: 0.1-1%

docs.title: Metadata Best Practices
docs.text:
Do Include: - Request IDs (for tracing) - User IDs (non-PII) - Environment (production/staging) - A/B test variant - Feature flags - Device/platform info

Don't Include: - PII (names, emails, addresses) - Sensitive data (SSN, passwords) - Large objects (>1KB)

Example: 

metadata={
    "request_id": "req-123456",
    "user_id": "usr-789012",  # Anonymized
    "environment": "production",
    "experiment": "model-v2-test",
    "variant": "treatment",
    "platform": "ios",
    "app_version": "3.2.1",
    "region": "us-west"
}

docs.title: Metrics Dashboard
docs.text: Real-time visibility into model performance.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: - Monitor model health - Track performance trends - Identify issues quickly - Make data-driven decisions

Key Metrics: - Performance (accuracy, precision, recall) - Volume (predictions/day) - Latency (response time) - Errors (failure rate)

docs.title: Where to see it
docs.text:
In the dashboard, this lives in Observability → Performance: platform health (Healthy, Degraded or Unhealthy), system performance over 7 days, 30 days, 90 days or 1 year, and Baseline Performance Metrics next to what has been measured since. See Observability.

The model list in the Model Register shows each system's verdicts and signals, and Needs Attention collects the alerts. Metrics you report yourself with client.metrics.create appear in Performance too.

docs.title: Classification Metrics
docs.text:
Binary Classification: - Accuracy - % correct predictions - Precision - True positives / (True positives + False positives) - Recall - True positives / (True positives + False negatives) - F1 Score - Harmonic mean of precision and recall - AUC-ROC - Area under ROC curve - AUC-PR - Area under Precision-Recall curve - Log Loss - Logarithmic loss

Multi-class Classification: - Macro-averaged metrics - Micro-averaged metrics - Per-class metrics - Confusion matrix

Confusion Matrix: 

              Predicted
              No   Yes
Actual  No   TN    FP
        Yes  FN    TP

Thresholds: - Adjust decision threshold - Optimize for precision or recall - View threshold impact

docs.title: Regression Metrics
docs.text:
• MAE - Mean Absolute Error
  • MSE - Mean Squared Error
  • RMSE - Root Mean Squared Error
  • R² Score - Coefficient of determination
  • MAPE - Mean Absolute Percentage Error
  • Median AE - Median Absolute Error

Visualizations: - Predicted vs Actual scatter plot - Residual plot - Error distribution histogram

docs.title: LLM Metrics
docs.text:
• Token Usage - Input/output tokens
  • Cost - Total spend, cost per request
  • Latency - Response time (p50, p95, p99)
  • Toxicity - Safety scores
  • RAG Quality - Retrieval/answer quality

docs.title: Custom Metrics
docs.text:
metric_type and metric_name are free text — log any business-specific number against a model, not just the built-in performance metrics:

client.metrics.create(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    metric_type="business",
    metric_name="revenue_impact",
    metric_value=12500.50,
)

# Or several at once (max 100 per call)
client.metrics.create_batch(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    metrics=[
        {"metric_type": "business", "metric_name": "revenue_impact", "metric_value": 12500.50},
        {"metric_type": "business", "metric_name": "cost_savings", "metric_value": 3200.00},
    ],
)

# Read them back
metrics = client.metrics.get_model_metrics(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    metric_type="business",
    start_date="2026-07-01",
    end_date="2026-07-31",
)

Common Custom Metrics: - Revenue impact - Cost savings - Customer satisfaction - Processing time - Business conversion rate

docs.title: Metric Aggregations
docs.text:
# Aggregated over a period — "daily", "weekly", etc.
client.metrics.aggregate(model_id="model-uuid", period="daily", metric_type="accuracy")

# Trend and rolling-window statistics
client.metrics.trend(model_id="model-uuid", metric_type="accuracy", lookback_days=30)
client.metrics.rolling(model_id="model-uuid", metric_type="accuracy", window_days=7)

# Raw time series over a required date range
client.metrics.timeseries(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    metric_type="accuracy",
    start_date="2026-07-01",
    end_date="2026-07-31",
)

# Everything for a model in one call
client.metrics.summary(model_id="model-uuid", days=30)

docs.title: Alerts on Metrics
docs.text:
Set thresholds to get notified:

client.alerts.create(
    name="Low Accuracy Alert",
    alert_type="performance",
    severity="high",
    model_id="model-uuid",
    conditions=[
        {"metric_name": "accuracy", "operator": "lt", "threshold": 0.85, "window_minutes": 60}
    ],
)

docs.title: Drift Detection
docs.text: Automatically detect when your data or model behavior changes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: - Identify when model needs retraining - Catch data quality issues - Maintain prediction accuracy - Compliance with model governance

Types of Drift: 1. Data Drift - Input distribution changes 2. Concept Drift - Feature-target relationship changes 3. Prediction Drift - Output distribution changes

docs.title: Data Drift
docs.text:
Definition: Changes in input feature distributions compared to training data.

Example: Income distribution shifted from mean $50k to $75k

Detection Methods:

Continuous Features: - Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) Test - Compares distributions - Population Stability Index (PSI) - Industry standard

Categorical Features: - Chi-squared Test - Compares frequency distributions - Jensen-Shannon (JS) Divergence - Symmetric KL divergence

docs.title: Configuring drift detection
docs.text:
Drift configuration is a REST-only surface today — there's no client.drift_config.* in the SDK yet, so this is curl rather than Python:

# Create a default config for a model
curl -X POST https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/drift-config/{model_id}/default \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WHITEBOX_API_KEY"

# Or the fastest path: apply a sensitivity preset directly
curl -X POST https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/drift-config/{model_id}/sensitivity/medium \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WHITEBOX_API_KEY"

Three presets ship — low, medium (recommended default), high — each setting the KS, chi-squared, JS, and PSI thresholds together along with the concept-drift and severity thresholds, rather than tuning each statistical test individually:

GET /api/v1/drift-config/presets                # all three, with their actual threshold values
GET /api/v1/drift-config/presets/{preset_name}   # one preset

For anything more specific than a preset, PUT /api/v1/drift-config/{model_id} takes the full feature_configs, concept_drift_config, alert_config, schedule_config, and threshold_config objects — see the response from GET /api/v1/drift-config/{model_id} for the exact shape a given model currently has.

Drift Score Interpretation: the medium preset's severity thresholds are a reasonable default reading — roughly 0.0–0.1 no meaningful drift, 0.1–0.3 worth investigating, 0.3+ action required — but the exact cutoffs are configurable per preset and per model rather than fixed platform-wide.

docs.title: Concept Drift
docs.text:
Definition: Changes in the relationship between features and target — the same input now predicts a different outcome than it used to.

Example: Credit score of 650 used to have a 20% default rate, now has 10%.

Detection approach: tracked via concept_drift_config on the same drift configuration above — performance-degradation-based (comparing recent vs. historical accuracy) and distribution-based methods, including ADWIN, are available as part of that config rather than as a separate endpoint.

docs.title: Prediction Drift
docs.text:
Definition: Changes in the model's output distribution, independent of whether the inputs changed — useful for catching a model that's started behaving differently even when the input population looks the same.

Example: Fraud-rate predictions increased from 5% to 15% of traffic.

docs.title: Drift Detection Dashboard
docs.text:
Drift Overview Page: - Models with drift - Recent drift events - Drift severity distribution - Timeline of detections

Per-Model Drift View: - Overall drift score - Per-feature drift scores - Distribution comparisons - Statistical test results - Recommended actions

docs.title: Drift Reports
docs.text:
Detailed Report Includes:

Summary: - Overall drift score - Number of drifted features - Severity classification - Detection date and time

Per-Feature Analysis: - Individual drift scores - Statistical test p-values - Distribution visualizations - Before/after statistics

Visualizations: - Distribution overlays (training vs production) - Time series of drift scores - Heatmap of feature drift over time

Recommendations: - Which features drifted most - Potential causes - Suggested actions

Example Report: 

Drift Detection Report
Model: Fraud Detection v2
Date: 2026-10-05

Overall Drift Score: 0.18 (Medium)

Drifted Features:
1. transaction_amount (High drift: 0.25)
   - Training: mean=$125, std=$50
   - Production: mean=$180, std=$75
   - Interpretation: Customers making larger purchases

2. merchant_category (Medium drift: 0.15)
   - New categories appearing: "crypto", "nft"
   - Training categories decreased: "travel"

3. time_of_day (Low drift: 0.08)
   - Slight shift toward evening transactions

Non-drifted Features:
- customer_age: 0.02
- account_age: 0.03

Recommendations:
✓ Retrain model with recent data (3+ months)
✓ Investigate new merchant categories
✓ Consider adding temporal features
✓ Update baseline after retraining

docs.title: Responding to Drift
docs.text:
Workflow:

1. Detection → Alert sent

2. Investigation: 

# List recent drift reports, most recent first
reports = client.drift.get_reports(model_id="model-uuid", limit=10)
latest = reports[0]

# Per-feature statistics live inside the report
for feature in latest["feature_drifts"]:
    print(f"{feature['feature_name']}: {feature['drift_score']} ({feature['severity']})")

# Trend over time, rather than a single snapshot
trend = client.drift.get_trend(model_id="model-uuid", days=30)

# Or run a fresh, ad-hoc check without waiting for the next scheduled one
result = client.drift.detect(model_id="model-uuid", window_size=1000)

Compare distributions visually on Assurance → Drift → Feature Analysis in the dashboard — there's no SDK method that hands back a chart object; feature_drifts above is the raw statistics behind it.

3. Action: - Low drift: Monitor, no action yet - Medium drift: Plan retraining within 1-2 weeks - High drift: Immediate retraining or model rollback

4. Retraining: 

# Register the retrained version under the same name
client.models.register(
    name="Fraud Detection",
    model_type="custom",
    version="2.3.0",
    features=feature_names,
    baseline_metrics={"accuracy": 0.91},  # New baselines
    tags=["retrained-drift-response"],
)

# Or, refreshing the same model's baseline after retraining in place
client.models.update_baseline(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    baseline_metrics={"accuracy": 0.94, "precision": 0.91},
)

docs.title: Drift Configuration Best Practices
docs.text:
Detection Frequency: - High-volume models: Daily - Medium-volume: Weekly - Low-volume: Monthly

Thresholds: - Start conservative: 0.2 (avoid false alarms) - Tune down: 0.1-0.15 (after baseline established) - Critical models: 0.05 (very sensitive)

Reference Period: - Training data: For long-term drift - Rolling window (30d): For recent trends - Both: Most comprehensive

docs.title: Explainability Engine
docs.text:
Understand why your models make specific predictions.

Looking for an explainability report, not the raw computation?

See Audit & Explanation Reports for how these explanations get packaged into something you can hand to a stakeholder or auditor.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: - Debug model decisions - Build trust with stakeholders - Regulatory compliance (right to explanation) - Identify biases - Model improvement insights

Supported Methods: - SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) - LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) - DiCE counterfactuals (what would have to change for a different outcome)

Explanations run your model

SHAP, LIME and DiCE explanations are computed by running the model itself, so WhiteBoxXAI needs the model file. Register the model through GitHub with storage_mode: full; scikit-learn-style pickle and joblib files are supported. For a model registered with metadata only, the explanation is recorded as failed, with a message saying no stored model artifact is available. Drift, fairness audits and reports don't need the model file.

Full method reference lives with the SDK

This section is the concepts and use cases. For the complete, verified method list — generate_bulk(), compare(), visualize()/visualize_multi(), set_config(), and every parameter — see SDK Documentation.

docs.title: SHAP Explanations
docs.text:
What is SHAP?

Based on game theory (Shapley values), SHAP provides: - Theoretically sound explanations - Local and global interpretability - Consistent feature attributions - Additive property

How it Works:

For each prediction: 1. Calculate the contribution of each feature 2. Base value (average prediction) + feature contributions = final prediction 3. Positive contribution = pushes the prediction higher 4. Negative contribution = pushes it lower

Generate a SHAP explanation:

explanation = client.explanations.generate(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    instance={"income": 75000, "credit_score": 780, "debt_ratio": 0.2, "age": 34},
    method="shap",
)

# Access results — this is a dict, not an object with attributes
print(f"Base value: {explanation['base_value']}")
print(f"Score: {explanation['score']}")

for feature, weight in explanation["feature_weights"].items():
    print(f"{feature}: {weight:+.3f}")

Waterfall Chart — shows cumulative feature contributions:

Base Value: 0.20
+ income (high): +0.15
+ credit_score (excellent): +0.25
+ debt_ratio (low): +0.10
- age (young): -0.05
= Final Prediction: 0.65

Get the chart-ready data behind it (not a rendered image — data for your own UI) with client.explanations.visualize(explanation_id, plot_type="waterfall"), or "force" for a force-plot layout of the same contributions.

docs.title: LIME Explanations
docs.text:
What is LIME?

Creates a simple, interpretable model around a specific prediction: 1. Generate perturbations around the instance 2. Get model predictions for perturbations 3. Train a simple linear model on these 4. Use the linear model's coefficients as the explanation

When to Use LIME: - Faster than SHAP for complex models - Good for high-dimensional data - Need quick explanations - Local understanding is sufficient

Generate a LIME explanation — the call is identical to SHAP's, just a different method:

explanation = client.explanations.generate(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    instance={"credit_score": 720, "income": 75000, "employment_years": 8, "debt_ratio": 0.35},
    method="lime",
    num_features=10,
)

for feature, weight in explanation["feature_weights"].items():
    direction = "increases" if weight > 0 else "decreases"
    print(f"{feature}: {abs(weight):.3f} {direction} the prediction")

Output Example: 

Prediction: Approved (probability: 0.85)

Top Contributing Features:
+ credit_score (720): +0.35 (high score increases approval)
+ income ($75k): +0.28 (sufficient income increases approval)
+ employment_years (8): +0.15 (stable employment increases approval)
- debt_ratio (0.35): -0.12 (moderate debt decreases approval)

docs.title: Global feature importance
docs.text:
There's no single endpoint that returns "global importance across all predictions" — aggregate it yourself from explanations you've already generated:

explanations = client.explanations.list_by_model(model_id="model-uuid", method="shap", limit=1000)

totals: dict[str, float] = {}
for exp in explanations:
    for feature, weight in exp["feature_weights"].items():
        totals[feature] = totals.get(feature, 0) + abs(weight)

ranked = sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)

Or, for a comparison across a specific set of already-generated explanations rather than a running total, client.explanations.compare(explanation_ids, comparison_type="feature_importance") does the aggregation server-side.

docs.title: Explanation Use Cases
docs.text:
1. Debugging — pull recent explanations for a model and look for one relying heavily on a feature that shouldn't matter:

recent = client.explanations.list_by_model(model_id="model-uuid", limit=100)

for exp in recent:
    top_feature = max(exp["feature_weights"], key=lambda f: abs(exp["feature_weights"][f]))
    if top_feature == "zip_code":  # shouldn't be driving decisions
        print(f"Investigate: {exp['id']} (prediction {exp['prediction_id']})")

2. Contestation — a customer disputes a denial; generate the explanation behind that specific prediction and hand it to them (or route it into a report for a formatted document):

explanation = client.explanations.generate(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    instance=denial_input_data,
    prediction_id=denial_prediction_id,
    method="shap",
)

3. Compliance — the same call, generated on demand for an audit request. It's automatically retained and searchable via list_by_model()/get_by_prediction() — there's no separate "audit metadata" field to set; the explanation itself is the record.

4. Model improvement — use the ranked list from Global feature importance above to spot low-importance features that might be candidates for removal.

docs.title: Explanation Configuration
docs.text:
Set per-model defaults — method, auto-generation, caching — with set_config():

client.explanations.set_config(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    default_method="shap_kernel",
    auto_explain=False,     # generate on-demand only
    cache_enabled=True,
    cache_ttl_hours=24,
)

docs.title: Bulk and async generation
docs.text:
For more than a handful of instances, generate_bulk() is non-blocking — you poll for results rather than waiting on the request:

job = client.explanations.generate_bulk(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    instances=[instance_1, instance_2, instance_3],
    method="shap",
)
# {"explanation_ids": [...], "total": 3, "message": "..."}

for explanation_id in job["explanation_ids"]:
    result = client.explanations.get(explanation_id)
    if result["status"] != "pending":
        print(result["feature_weights"])

generate_async() is the single-instance equivalent — same non-blocking, poll-with-get() pattern, for one instance at a time.

docs.title: Bias Detection
docs.text:
Audit models for fairness across demographic groups.

Need a bias audit report you can hand to an auditor?

See Audit & Explanation Reports — the fairness results below feed directly into the Bias audit report category.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: - Ensure fair treatment across groups - Regulatory compliance (ECOA, Fair Housing Act, etc.) - Ethical AI practices - Mitigate reputational risk

Key Capabilities: - Multi-metric fairness assessment - Protected attribute analysis - Bias severity classification - Mitigation recommendations

docs.title: Fairness Metrics
docs.text:
1. Demographic Parity (Statistical Parity)

Definition: Positive prediction rates should be equal across groups.

Formula: P(Ŷ=1 | A=a) = P(Ŷ=1 | A=b) for all groups a, b

Example: 

Loan approval rates should be similar:
- Male: 65%
- Female: 63%
- Ratio: 0.97 (PASS - within 0.8-1.2)

When to Use: When equal outcomes are the goal

2. Equal Opportunity

Definition: True positive rates should be equal across groups.

Formula: P(Ŷ=1 | Y=1, A=a) = P(Ŷ=1 | Y=1, A=b)

Example: 

Among qualified applicants, approval rates should be equal:
- Male (qualified): 85% approved
- Female (qualified): 87% approved
- Difference: 0.02 (PASS - < 0.1)

When to Use: When equal opportunity for qualified individuals matters

3. Equalized Odds

Definition: Both TPR and FPR should be equal across groups.

Formula: P(Ŷ=1 | Y=y, A=a) = P(Ŷ=1 | Y=y, A=b) for y ∈ {0,1}

Example: 

TPR equal + FPR equal:
- TPR: Male 85%, Female 83% (diff: 0.02 ✓)
- FPR: Male 12%, Female 14% (diff: 0.02 ✓)
- PASS

When to Use: Strictest criterion, both false positives and false negatives matter

4. Disparate Impact

Definition: Ratio of positive outcomes between groups.

Formula: Disparate Impact = P(Ŷ=1 | A=unprivileged) / P(Ŷ=1 | A=privileged)

Legal Standard: Must be ≥ 0.8 (80% rule in US)

Example: 

Female approval: 52%
Male approval: 65%
DI = 52/65 = 0.80 (PASS - exactly at threshold)

docs.title: Running Fairness Audits
docs.text:
From the dashboard:

There is no form to fill in. On the Classic layout's Bias & Fairness page, Run Fairness Audit opens a short guide. An audit compares outcomes across groups, so it needs the true outcomes, the model's predictions and each record's group membership, and WhiteBoxXAI doesn't hold that data. Audits are submitted from where the data lives, with the SDK or POST /api/v1/fairness/audit. The results then appear in Assurance → Fairness (or the Classic page): Fairness Metrics, Group Comparison, Audit Results and Recommendations.

Via SDK:

audit() isn't a data-source query the way drift detection is — it doesn't fetch predictions for you. You supply the true labels, predicted labels, and each row's group membership; the platform computes the fairness metrics from that. A common pattern is pulling logged predictions first, then joining in whatever demographic data you have:

predictions = client.predictions.query(model_id="model-uuid", start_time="2026-07-01T00:00:00Z")

# predictions.query() gives you what the model predicted, not the actual outcome or
# demographic group — join both in from your own records, keyed by prediction_id
y_pred = [p["output_data"]["prediction"] for p in predictions]
y_true = [your_ground_truth[p["prediction_id"]] for p in predictions]
gender = [your_demographics[p["prediction_id"]]["gender"] for p in predictions]

audit = client.fairness.audit(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    sensitive_attributes=["gender"],
    y_true=y_true,
    y_pred=y_pred,
    group_data={"gender": gender},
    metrics_to_compute=["demographic_parity", "equal_opportunity", "equalized_odds", "disparate_impact"],
)

# This is a dict, not an object — same as every other SDK response
print(f"Fairness score: {audit['overall_fairness_score']:.2f}")
print(f"Bias detected: {audit['bias_detected']}")

for metric_name, result in audit["results"].items():
    print(f"{metric_name}: {result['score']:.3f} ({'PASS' if result['passed'] else 'FAIL'})")

for rec in audit["recommendations"]:
    print(f"- {rec}")

Pass more than one attribute in sensitive_attributes — and a matching key in group_data for each — to audit several protected attributes in one call, rather than needing separate calls per attribute.

docs.title: Understanding Audit Results
docs.text:
overall_fairness_score: 0.0–1.0 (the dashboard shows it as a percentage) - 0.90–1.00: Excellent (very fair) - 0.80–0.89: Good (acceptable for most use cases) - 0.70–0.79: Fair (attention needed) - 0.60–0.69: Poor (action required) - < 0.60: Critical (immediate action)

Example Audit Report:

Fairness Audit Report
Model: Loan Approval Model v2.1
Date: 2026-10-05 14:30 UTC
Protected Attribute: Gender
Reference Group: Male
Comparison Group: Female

Overall Fairness Score: 0.75 (Fair)

Detailed Results:

1. Demographic Parity: FAIL (0.72)
   Male approval rate: 65.2%
   Female approval rate: 46.9%
   Ratio: 0.72 (should be 0.8-1.2)
   Severity: HIGH

2. Equal Opportunity: PASS (0.88)
   Male TPR (qualified approved): 87.3%
   Female TPR (qualified approved): 76.5%
   Ratio: 0.88 (should be > 0.8)
   Severity: LOW

3. Equalized Odds: FAIL
   TPR Difference: 0.11 (HIGH)
   FPR Difference: 0.15 (HIGH)
   Both should be < 0.1
   Severity: HIGH

4. Disparate Impact: FAIL (0.72)
   Should be ≥ 0.8 (80% rule)
   Legal compliance: AT RISK
   Severity: CRITICAL

Root Cause Analysis:
- Feature "income" strongly correlated with gender (0.45)
- Training data: 65% male, 35% female (imbalanced)
- Historical bias in labels possible

Recommendations:
1. URGENT: Review for legal compliance (DI < 0.8)
2. Retrain with balanced dataset
3. Consider removing/debiasing correlated features
4. Apply fairness constraints during training
5. Adjust decision thresholds per group
6. Consult legal/compliance team

Action Items:
☐ Share with compliance team
☐ Schedule retraining
☐ Implement mitigation strategy
☐ Re-audit after changes

docs.title: Multi-Attribute Audits
docs.text:
As shown above, sensitive_attributes already takes a list — auditing gender, race, and age together is one call, not a separate multi-attribute method:

audit = client.fairness.audit(
    model_id="model-uuid",
    sensitive_attributes=["gender", "race", "age_group"],
    y_true=y_true,
    y_pred=y_pred,
    group_data={"gender": gender, "race": race, "age_group": age_group},
)

For intersectional analysis — fairness across combinations like (Male, White) vs. (Female, Black) rather than each attribute independently — construct a combined group column yourself (f"{gender}_{race}") and pass it as its own entry in sensitive_attributes/group_data; there's no separate endpoint that cross-tabulates attributes automatically.

docs.title: Bias Mitigation Strategies
docs.text:
WhiteBoxXAI's job here is diagnosis — the audit above tells you which metric failed and by how much. Fixing it is a modeling decision that happens in your own training pipeline, using whatever fairness-aware tooling you already use (or a library like Fairlearn or AIF360):

  • Pre-processing: rebalance or reweight training data, and check for features correlated with the protected attribute (a proxy like ZIP code standing in for race) before training.
  • In-processing: train with a fairness constraint (e.g. Fairlearn's ExponentiatedGradient) if your protected attribute is available at training time.
  • Post-processing: adjust decision thresholds per group, and evaluate the tradeoff against overall performance before shipping it.

Whichever you use, re-run client.fairness.audit() against the retrained or adjusted model to confirm the fix actually worked — see Explanation Use Cases above for the same "verify against real computed data, not before-the-fact assumptions" pattern applied to explanations.

docs.title: Continuous Fairness Monitoring
docs.text:
Trend and history, without re-running a full audit each time:

client.fairness.get_bias_history(model_id="model-uuid", days=30)
client.fairness.get_metric_history(model_id="model-uuid", metric_type="demographic_parity", days=30)
client.fairness.get_latest_audit(model_id="model-uuid")

Alert when fairness drops:

client.alerts.create(
    name="Fairness Score Alert",
    alert_type="bias",
    severity="high",
    model_id="model-uuid",
    conditions=[
        {"metric_name": "disparate_impact_ratio", "operator": "lt", "threshold": 0.8, "window_minutes": 10080}
    ],
    notification_channels=[{"type": "email", "target": "compliance@example.com"}],
)

There's no built-in scheduler for re-running an audit itself on a cadence — audit() needs ground truth and group data you supply, so "run this weekly" means your own scheduled job calling it, not a platform-side schedule. Governance Review Boards' automated periodic reviews are the closest built-in equivalent if what you actually want is a recurring human review rather than a recurring computation.

docs.title: LLM Monitoring
docs.text:
Token, cost, latency, safety, and RAG-quality tracking for LLM calls — the LLM equivalent of prediction logging above. For the dashboard walkthrough, see Observability → LLM & RAG; this section is the SDK surface behind it. For every provider you can log from, see LLM monitoring.

client.llm.log_call(
    provider="openai",
    model_name="gpt-4o",
    prompt="Summarize this customer complaint...",
    completion="The customer is reporting...",
    latency_ms=842,
    prompt_tokens=120,
    completion_tokens=45,
    model_id="model-uuid",   # optional — associates the call with a registered model
)

# Cost, latency, and volume, aggregated
client.llm.usage_stats(start_time="2026-07-01T00:00:00Z", end_time="2026-07-31T23:59:59Z")
client.llm.cost_breakdown()
client.llm.trends_tokens(model_id="model-uuid", granularity="day")

# Safety — toxicity, PII, and harmful-content scoring on a piece of content
client.safety.analyze(content="...")

# RAG retrieval quality — pass ground_truth_ids to get precision/recall/MRR/NDCG computed
# server-side at log time
client.rag.log_retrieval(
    query="What's our refund policy?",
    results=[{"document_id": "doc-1", "rank": 1, "score": 0.92}],
    top_k=5,
    retrieval_method="vector",
    model_id="model-uuid",
)
client.rag.get_stats(model_id="model-uuid")

client.llm, client.safety, and client.rag are each their own resource with a larger method surface than shown here (batch logging, threshold-based alerting, trend queries) — see the MCP Server tool reference for the equivalent tool list, which mirrors the SDK method-for-method.

docs.title: Alert System
docs.text: Covered in Needs Attention and the Alerts API reference. Active rules are evaluated automatically when metrics are logged, drift reports are created and bias audits complete; see When rules are evaluated. This page's Alerts on Metrics and Continuous Fairness Monitoring sections above show it applied to specific features.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Covered in full in Reports: 12 report types, templates, branding, sign-off, auditor share links and schedules. Ids and data requirements are in the Report types reference.

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text: Covered in Compliance frameworks (what WhiteBoxXAI records for each of the five frameworks), Compliance & Evidence (controls, evidence and the audit trail) and Reviews & Decisions (approval workflows and the decision archive).

docs.title: Reviews & Decisions
docs.text:
Governance Review Boards bring executive oversight to your AI models through multi-party approval workflows, AI-assisted review templates, a searchable decision archive, and automated periodic reviews. Use them to make sure the right people sign off before a model goes to production — and to keep an auditable record of every decision.

In the Enhanced Dashboard this is Reviews & Decisions (g then v), with five tabs:

Tab Shows My reviews Requests waiting for your decision Requests Every request, filterable by status (Draft, Submitted, Under review, Approved, Denied, Withdrawn, Archived) and type Boards Your review boards, with their Members, Rules, Activity and Schedules Decisions The searchable decision archive, with Export CSV (up to 10,000 rows) RACI Who's Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed, per board

You can also automate most of it through the REST API. API examples below use the base URL https://api.whiteboxxai.com and an API key (Authorization: Bearer $WHITEBOX_API_KEY). Voting and finalizing are the exception: they need a person's own signed-in session and an authenticator code. See Vote with an authenticator code.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
Review board — a group of people who vote on requests, with configurable voting rules (approval threshold, quorum, and optional weighted or unanimous voting).

Review request — something that needs approval (for example, deploying a model), submitted to a board for a vote.

Decision — a member's vote on a request: approve, deny, abstain, or request changes.

Archive — every finalized decision is stored with an executive summary and is full-text searchable for later audits.

docs.title: Board types
docs.text: Type Use for technical Technical architecture reviews business Business impact assessments compliance Regulatory compliance reviews executive C-level strategic decisions

docs.title: Request types
docs.text: model_deployment, architecture_change, policy_update, risk_assessment, compliance_review.

docs.title: Priority levels
docs.text: low, medium, high, critical.

docs.title: Create a board
docs.text:
In the dashboard, an administrator goes to Reviews & Decisions → Boards → New board, or uses the API:

curl -X POST https://api.whiteboxxai.com/api/v1/governance/review-boards \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WHITEBOX_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "AI Ethics Committee",
    "description": "Reviews high-risk AI deployments",
    "board_type": "compliance",
    "approval_threshold": 66,
    "quorum_required": 3
  }'

docs.title: Voting rules
docs.text:
• approval_threshold — percentage of votes needed to approve (e.g. 66 for a two-thirds majority).
  • requires_unanimous — if true, every vote must be approve.
  • quorum_required — minimum number of votes before a request can be finalized.
  • voting_power — per-member weight, for weighted voting.

docs.title: Add board members
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/governance/review-boards/{board_id}/members
{
  "user_id": "...",
  "role": "member",
  "voting_power": 1.0
}

Roles determine what a member can do:

  • Observers — read-only, cannot vote.
  • Members — can vote and comment.
  • Chairs — full board management, including finalizing decisions.

docs.title: Governance guarantees
docs.text: Three rules are enforced at the database layer, not just in the application. That distinction matters in an audit: "show me the schema" is a stronger answer than "trust our code," and it means the rules hold even for a caller that bypasses the application entirely.

docs.title: Separation of duties
docs.text:
A request's submitter cannot vote on their own request. This is enforced by the platform on every write path, so it can't be circumvented by calling the API directly rather than using the dashboard. A member can also only cast one vote per request.

This is the property that makes a review board governance rather than an approval button — and it's why a "zero self-approvals" statement about your organization is provable rather than asserted.

docs.title: Vote changes are recorded, never overwritten
docs.text:
A member may change their vote while a request is still open. When they do, the previous vote is preserved in an append-only vote history rather than being replaced. Nothing about a vote's history is silently lost.

Once a request is finalized, votes are closed.

docs.title: The decision archive is immutable
docs.text:
Finalized decisions cannot be edited or deleted — edits and deletions are refused for both the archive and the vote history, including through the API.

If a decision was recorded in error, you don't mutate history. You record a correction: a new archive entry that supersedes the original, carrying a reference to it (supersedes_id) and a correction_reason. Both entries remain, and the chain between them is explicit — which is exactly what an auditor wants to see.

docs.title: AI-generated content is labeled
docs.text: Where WhiteBoxXAI drafts content for a board — review templates, best-practice suggestions, decision summaries — that output is labeled as AI-generated pending human sign-off. An approval is never allowed to look like a human judgement when it was substantively AI-authored.

docs.title: Submit and vote on a request
docs.text:
Optionally start from an AI-generated template, then create the request:

# 1. Generate an AI review template
POST /api/v1/governance/review-boards/ai/generate-template
{
  "review_type": "model_deployment",
  "board_id": "...",
  "context": { "model_name": "Fraud Detection v3.0", "model_version": "3.0.1" }
}

# 2. Create the request
POST /api/v1/governance/review-boards/requests
{
  "board_id": "...",
  "title": "Deploy Fraud Detection v3.0",
  "description": "<review details>",
  "request_type": "model_deployment",
  "priority": "high"
}

Submit the request to open it for voting, or withdraw it if it's no longer needed:

POST /api/v1/governance/review-boards/requests/{request_id}/submit
POST /api/v1/governance/review-boards/requests/{request_id}/withdraw

Members cast votes from the request's slide-over in Reviews & Decisions: Approve, Deny, Abstain or Request changes, with a Justification and optional Conditions. The panel shows the approval weight so far (Approval weight: X of Y needed) and whether quorum is met.

docs.title: Vote with an authenticator code
docs.text:
A vote is a sign-off that ends up in an immutable archive, so it has to be provably yours and made against evidence you actually saw:

  • Two-factor authentication must be on. Without it, the vote is refused with "Voting and sign-off need two-factor authentication. Turn it on in Settings > Security, then try again."
  • Each vote and each finalization needs a current authenticator code (or one of your backup codes), entered in the Authenticator code field. Repeated wrong codes lock voting for a while and are recorded in the audit trail.
  • It must be your own session. Organization API keys can't vote or finalize, so neither can an automated pipeline or an AI agent acting with a key.
  • The evidence must not have changed. Every request has an evidence snapshot hash. A vote carries the hash of the version you reviewed, and if the request changed after you opened it, the vote is refused: "This request changed after you opened it. Reload it and review the current version before voting."

Over the API, from a person's own session:

POST /api/v1/governance/review-boards/requests/{request_id}/decisions
{
  "decision": "approve",
  "justification": "Model meets all compliance requirements.",
  "conditions": "Re-run the fairness audit after the next retrain.",
  "evidence_snapshot_hash": "<from the request detail you reviewed>",
  "totp_code": "123456"
}

AI assistants can prepare and summarise a request's dossier for you through the MCP server, and in hosts that support interactive cards can show you voting buttons, but the vote is still yours, made with your session and your code.

A vote from the request's own submitter is rejected — see Separation of duties.

Check status at any time:

GET /api/v1/governance/review-boards/requests/{request_id}/status
# -> total_members, votes_cast, approve_count, threshold_met, quorum_met, can_finalize

Board members can see what's waiting on them:

GET /api/v1/governance/review-boards/my-reviews
GET /api/v1/governance/review-boards/{board_id}/dashboard

In the dashboard, these are the My reviews tab and the board's slide-over on the Boards tab.

A request can be finalized once both quorum and the approval threshold are met, by an administrator or the board's chair. Finalizing is the formal sign-off, so it needs an authenticator code too. It creates an archive entry with an AI-generated executive summary:

POST /api/v1/governance/review-boards/requests/{request_id}/finalize
{ "totp_code": "123456" }

A denied review becomes a tracked risk

Denying a request, or sending it back with request changes, automatically drafts an entry in your AI Risk Register so the concern is owned and tracked rather than left in a vote record. See Automatic risk drafting.

docs.title: Requests in the dashboard
docs.text:
Requests → Raise a review request opens the request form. Generate AI Template drafts the description from the request type and system, and AI-drafted text stays marked "AI-generated content — pending human sign-off" until a person edits it. Choose Save as draft or Save and submit.

A request's slide-over has everything a reviewer needs in one place:

  • Submit to the board, Withdraw and Finalize the decision
  • Votes, with approval weight and quorum (see voting)
  • Discussion: comments typed as Discussion, Question, Concern, Suggestion, Approval note or Denial reason, with replies
  • Attachments: PDF, PNG, JPG, CSV, Markdown or text files, such as an architecture diagram or a test report. The requester, board members and administrators can attach files until a decision is made.
  • RACI assignments
  • AI Governance Suggestions and AI Best Practices for the request type

docs.title: Boards
docs.text: On the Boards tab, administrators create boards (New board), add members with a role, voting power, department and expertise, and edit the rules: quorum, approval weight, the escalation board and how often reviews recur. Boards can be deactivated and reactivated. Everyone can see a board's Members, Rules, Activity and Schedules.

docs.title: RACI assignment
docs.text:
Beyond a vote, a review request can carry a RACI assignment — who's Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed — the structure ISO/IEC 42001 Clause 5.3 and Annex A.3 expect for AI governance roles and responsibilities.

In the dashboard, this is the RACI tab of Reviews & Decisions: a per-board matrix of requests against members, with R, A, C and I assignments drawn from the board's real membership. Assign roles from a request's slide-over.

GET  /api/v1/governance/review-boards/raci-grid       # the full grid, optionally filtered to one board
